visual.title: Six labelled steps: turning a spoken complaint into a defensible description
visual.description: A sequence diagram for the description-first method: each step names the action, the artifact it produces, and the failure it prevents. The diagram is a reasoning sequence, not a recording of anyone's appointment.
steps: Step 1 — Elicit: ask an open question and write down the person's own wording while they speak. Artifact: a quotation. Failure prevented: the substitution of a technical term for the material it replaced.

Step 2 — Separate theme from mode: for each reported experience, record what it is about (content) and how it is given (form) in two distinct clauses. Artifact: a two-part description. Failure prevented: losing the mode, which is where much of the classificatory weight sits.

Step 3 — Suspend the diagnostic question: bracket, for this portion of the interview, the question of what the description means clinically, and record the person's own goal in their words. Artifact: a statement of the activity the person wants back. Failure prevented: a plan organised around a symptom the person never asked to lose.

Step 4 — Mark the boundary: label anything that is an inference as an inference, with the observations it rests on, or delete it. Artifact: a note in which description and inference are visually distinguishable. Failure prevented: the reader treating a judgement as a finding.

Step 5 — Check the record against the person: read a short summary back and record the corrections. Artifact: corrected wording. Failure prevented: a description so firmly the clinician's own that the informant cannot amend it.

Step 6 — State the undecided: name one question the record cannot answer and what would move it. Artifact: an explicit unknown with a revision condition. Failure prevented: false closure, where a rich description is mistaken for an explanation.

lessons.title: Self-disorder research: how a phenomenological concept becomes a measured one
lessons.explanation:
Last lesson's method produced descriptions. This lesson follows one description-originating concept all the way into instruments, samples and statistics, because that journey is where most of the confusion about psychiatric 'biomarkers of experience' is created. Education only; nothing here diagnoses a person or advises on treatment.

The concept is basic or minimal self-disorder, sometimes called ipseity disturbance: a change not in what a person believes or feels, but in the felt status of being the one to whom their experience is happening. A 2021 review by the originators of the main instrument describes the notion of disordered self in schizophrenia as appearing early in the literature, records that Psychopathology published the psychometric instrument the Examination of Anomalous Self-Experience (EASE) in 2005, and explains the notion of the disorder of basic or minimal self with the help of phenomenological philosophy before describing the clinical manifestations the instrument targets [1]. The same review states the authors' conclusion that basic self-disorder represents a crucial phenotype of schizophrenia spectrum disorders and a potential avenue for pathogenetic research and psychotherapeutic treatment [1]. That conclusion is the position of researchers who built the instrument, and it should be read as an argued position rather than a settled finding.

The instrument is a coding scheme, not a questionnaire. EASE is administered as a semi-structured interview by a trained clinician who must make a judgement about whether a described experience instantiates a particular anomaly. Everything that lesson 65 said about instruments applies, with an extra turn of the screw: here the instrument does not measure the person's self-report so much as the interviewer's ability to elicit and code a specific kind of description. That is why training and calibration matter, and why an 'EASE score' in one study is not automatically commensurable with one in another.

The empirical record is real and worth taking seriously. In a study of 100 first-admission psychiatric inpatients, self-disorders aggregated significantly in the schizophrenia spectrum disorders, with no difference between schizophrenia and schizotypal disorders; EASE scores correlated moderately with canonical psychopathological dimensions of schizophrenia; factor analysis disclosed only one factor; and internal consistency was excellent [3]. The authors conclude that self-disorders aggregate selectively in the schizophrenia spectrum and that the study lends validity to the view of self-disorder as an experiential vulnerability phenotype [3].

Then the early-detection claim. In a study of 49 people at ultra-high risk for psychosis and 52 matched healthy controls, assessed with EASE and followed for a mean of 569 days, EASE total scores were significantly higher in the ultra-high-risk group, and Cox regression indicated that total EASE score significantly predicted time to transition to psychotic disorder when other significant predictors were controlled for [4]. Exploratory analyses found higher basic self-disturbance scores in schizophrenia-spectrum cases irrespective of whether they transitioned [4]. The authors present this as a way of further 'closing in' on individuals truly at high risk, particularly of schizophrenia-spectrum disorder [4].

Now the discipline this level is trying to build: separating what those results establish from what they are often taken to establish. A construct can have excellent internal consistency (its items hang together), a single factor (one dimension underlies them), and higher scores in a diagnostic group, and still be neither specific to that group nor useful for predicting individual outcomes. Internal consistency is a property of the instrument, group difference is a property of a sample, and prediction in a small cohort is a claim about that cohort's follow-up, not about the person in the next chair.

The critical literature makes this concrete. A clarification paper on minimal-self disturbance notes that there is no doubt that disturbances of the narrative self and metacognition are also important in schizophrenia-spectrum conditions, but that it is unclear how specific such disturbances are to schizophrenia-spectrum conditions or to psychosis more broadly; it records that no studies of that dimension had compared schizophrenia with other forms of psychosis, and points to extensive work showing comparable deficits in borderline personality disorder [2]. The same paper lists the questions still open, including specificity, internal structure and pathogenesis, and ways in which the concept overlaps with subjective changes described in psychotic depression, mania, depersonalisation and heightened introspection [2]. Read those two papers side by side and you have the shape of the field: a research programme with a coherent construct, a working instrument, encouraging group-level findings, and unresolved specificity.
lessons.example:
Worked reasoning on a fictional monitoring scenario, to show what the evidence can and cannot support.

A fictional early-intervention service decides to add EASE assessment to its intake for all referrals aged 15-30 with attenuated psychotic symptoms. The clinical lead writes a memo claiming the change will 'identify who will develop psychosis'.

What the cited evidence actually supports: in one cohort of 49 ultra-high-risk participants with a mean follow-up of about eighteen months, higher total EASE scores were associated with shorter time to transition in a model controlling for other significant predictors, and the construct showed graded levels across diagnostic groups in a separate inpatient sample [3][4]. Both are group-level observations in specific samples. What the memo's claim requires: a calibrated threshold, an estimate of how many people above that threshold will transition and how many will not, and evidence that the instrument adds information beyond cheaper assessment. None of those is in the two papers.

Now the sharper problem — moving from 'higher in schizophrenia spectrum' to 'specific to schizophrenia spectrum'. In the 100-admission study, the comparison of interest was between diagnostic groups within a heterogeneous inpatient sample [3]. Diagnostic groups were formed using current criteria, and the construct is then described as a phenotype of that spectrum. This is not fraud and it is not circular in a worthless sense: a construct can validly describe a category it was derived alongside. But it does mean that a study of this design cannot answer a question about specificity against conditions the sample barely contains, and one of the critical papers says exactly that such comparisons are missing for related dimensions [2].

Practical implication, transferable to any instrument: before adopting a measure, write down three numbers you would need — prevalence of the outcome in the measured group, the proportion of those above the cut-off who reach the outcome, and the proportion below it who do. If no study gives all three in a population like yours, the measure is a research tool, not a triage decision. That is not a reason to be dismissive; it is the difference between using a construct to think with and using it to allocate a scarce service.
lessons.question: A colleague says: 'Self-disorder research shows the EASE measures the core vulnerability of schizophrenia, so a high EASE score identifies who will develop it.' Using the sources in this lesson, what is the most accurate correction?
lessons.answer: The evidence supports self-disorders as a construct that aggregates in schizophrenia-spectrum groups and, in one small ultra-high-risk cohort, predicted time to transition when other predictors were controlled; it does not supply the thresholds and outcome proportions needed to identify an individual's future, and specificity against other conditions remains contested by the field's own critical literature.
lessons.distractor: The EASE has not been empirically studied, so no claim about it can be made at all beyond the authors' personal impressions.
lessons.correction: The second answer over-corrects into dismissal and misstates the record: there are published studies with internal-consistency, factor-structure and group-comparison results [3], and a prospective ultra-high-risk study with a Cox model [4]. The first answer is the correction that does justice to both the evidence and its limits. Two additional facts are needed to move from 'associated with' to 'identifies': the predictive values at a chosen threshold in a comparable population, and evidence that the instrument beats simpler information. The lesson's critical source also notes that specificity of closely related disturbances against other conditions has either not been tested or has been called into question, which is why the strongest defensible statement is about a research phenotype rather than an individual forecast.

depth.definitions:
Ipseity (also called minimal or basic self): the pre-reflective sense of being the subject of one's own experience, as distinct from the narrative self, the story a person tells about who they are. Basic self-disorder or self-disorder: anomalies in that minimal sense, for example experiences of thoughts, feelings or actions as strangely external, mechanical or not fully one's own. EASE (Examination of Anomalous Self-Experience): a semi-structured, interview-based instrument published in 2005 that codes such anomalies [1]. Internal consistency: the degree to which items of a scale cohere; it is a property of the instrument, not evidence of validity. Factor structure: how many underlying dimensions the items appear to measure. Concurrent validity: agreement with an existing standard. Predictive value: the probability of an outcome given a test result, which requires the outcome's base rate (lesson 65 did this arithmetic). Ultra-high risk (UHR): a research designation for people with attenuated or brief limited symptoms and/or genetic risk, not a diagnosis.

Prerequisite: lesson 71 for description-first method and the form/content distinction; lesson 65 for what instruments do and do not establish; lesson 43 for the lifespan framing of neurodevelopmental and vulnerability constructs.
depth.mechanism:
The mechanism of the research programme is a chain with four links, and each link can break. Link one: a description of an anomaly is written down in enough detail that another clinician can recognise it. Link two: the descriptions are standardised into items with anchor examples, so that two trained raters converge. Link three: scores are compared across diagnostic groups and used to predict an outcome. Link four: group-level findings are offered as clinically usable knowledge.

Link one to two is where most information is lost, because the item must be recognisable to a rater who never met the original patient. Link two to three imports all the standard problems of small samples, selection into follow-up, and outcomes defined by the same categories used to select participants: in the 100-admission study the groups were formed by diagnosis and the construct was then assessed [3]; in the UHR study the outcome was transition to psychotic disorder, defined by an interview-based threshold, and only 49 people were followed [4]. Link three to four is the largest jump, and it is not made by any of these papers: prediction in a cohort with a specified follow-up does not transfer to individual decision-making without thresholds and validation in the target population, a point the general clinical-inference literature and the level's later lessons on evidence (75-78) will make repeatedly.

Two further mechanisms are worth naming. First, a construct derived inside a category inherits the category's arguable boundaries. If schizotypal disorder is inside the spectrum by definition, then finding self-disorders in it as well as in schizophrenia is partly a statement about the boundary, not only about the biology; the study's own finding of no difference between the two is interesting precisely because it bears on whether the boundary is natural [3]. Second, the direction of the research community's investment matters: EASE's developers are the authors of the main review and of the studies that support it [1][3]. That does not make the results false, and lesson 65 already recorded the same fact about another instrument; it means the burden of independent replication is real.
depth.secondExample:
A contrasting application, moving the same reasoning to a concept with the opposite problem — too much specificity and not enough construct clarity.

Consider the classical construct of 'loss of vital contact with reality', or the simpler phrase 'she is not herself', both of which describe a global change in how someone's presence registers with others. Unlike self-disorders, these have no standard instrument: there is no anchor set, no training procedure, no score. The result is that two clinicians can agree in conversation that a person has changed in this way and mean different things, and nothing accumulates across settings.

Put the two concepts side by side and the trade-off is visible. The EASE construct sacrificed some of the immediacy of 'not herself' in order to gain codability, and in doing so it gained results — internal consistency, factor structure, group differences, a prediction model [3][4] — while taking on the risks of any coding scheme: it can only capture what an instrument trained on descriptions can elicit, and its apparent specificity is bounded by the samples studied. The unstructured construct lost nothing in richness and gained nothing in evidence.

The transferable rule for reading any psychiatric construct: ask whether the loss happened in the direction of evidence (a narrower claim that can be checked) or in the direction of authority (a technical term that discourages checking). Self-disorder research is a defensible example of the first; the lesson 63 warning about translating 'hostile' into 'guarded affect' is an example of the second.
depth.mistake:
Misconception one: that a phenomenological construct is unfalsifiable, so self-disorder research is philosophy in clinical clothing. In fact the construct generated specific, checkable predictions, and some of them were tested: it was assessed against diagnostic groups, correlated with established symptom dimensions, analysed for factor structure, and used in a prospective prediction model [3][4]. Falsifiability is not the problem here; transfer to individual prediction is.

Misconception two, more damaging in practice: that if a measure is 'core', it is specific. Core means central to the phenomenon under study, not exclusive to it. The clarificatory paper explicitly notes that closely related disturbances (narrative self, metacognition) are found in borderline personality disorder and that their specificity for schizophrenia-spectrum conditions or psychosis broadly is unclear, and it calls for comparisons that had not been done [2]. A clinician who reasons 'core, therefore specific, therefore diagnostic' has made two unsupported inferences on the basis of one word.

Misconception three: that a validated instrument yields a valid answer for any person. Every instrument in this literature depends on the person being able to describe experience and the interviewer being able to elicit it; the original clinical argument for description-first method includes the observation that some people conceal experiences they consider strange or shameful, which is a systematic reason for under-detection rather than random noise. Diagnostic correction: when a score is low, ask whether the person did not have the experience or did not say.
depth.application:
Nonblocking task. You are given a fictional abstract-like summary: 'In 64 first-episode patients, a self-disorder interview score was higher in the group later diagnosed with a schizophrenia-spectrum disorder than in the group diagnosed with a mood disorder (p = 0.02). Scores correlated with a global functioning measure (r = 0.31).' Write a 150-word appraisal with exactly four labelled sentences: what the study supports; what it does not support; the information missing before it could guide a service; and one confound.

Model response. What it supports: a group-level association between higher self-disorder scores and a schizophrenia-spectrum outcome in this sample, consistent with the aggregation reported in the 100-admission inpatient study [3]. What it does not support: any individual-level prediction, because no threshold, no sensitivity or specificity, and no outcome base rate are given, and the design (score and then later diagnosis) cannot rule out that the score reflected features of the outcome category definition itself. Missing information: in a service seeing a given mix of presentations, the proportion with a high score who later receive the spectrum diagnosis and the proportion with a low score who do; plus whether the assessment adds anything beyond a standard diagnostic interview. One confound: raters were not blind to the emerging clinical picture, as in most interview-based designs, so expectancy about which patients 'look' like spectrum cases can inflate the association; a second defensible answer is that r = 0.31 with a functioning measure means the score explains a small share of variation in functioning.

Rubric: 1 point for keeping the supported claim to group level; 1 for naming a missing quantity needed for prediction; 1 for a confound that is specific to this design (blinding, selection, or criterion circularity) rather than generic; 1 for not using the words 'biomarker' or 'diagnostic test' without qualification. Three or four points means the evidence-to-claim distance is being tracked; two or fewer usually means the p value was read as a magnitude, which it is not.
depth.summary:
A phenomenological description became a construct (basic self-disorder), then an instrument (EASE, 2005), then a body of group-level findings, then a contender for early detection [1][3][4]. Each transformation is visible in the record: constructs can be checked, instruments can be scored, groups can be compared — and each step adds assumptions that the next reader has to inspect. The critical literature is part of the field, not an attack on it: specificity against borderline personality disorder and across psychoses is unresolved, and the concept overlaps with subjective changes in other conditions [2].

Transfer: the pattern you just learned — description, coding scheme, group difference, individual promise — recurs in every 'measure of the core feature' you will meet, including digital phenotyping, inflammatory markers and neuroimaging classifiers. The two questions to carry are: what exactly is coded, and what was the outcome base rate in a population like mine? The next lesson moves from one construct to measurement in general: what a published scale actually claims when it reports reliability, validity and a change score.

readings.title: Disordered Selfhood in Schizophrenia and the Examination of Anomalous Self-Experience (2021 review) — PMC8686724
readings.note: Written by researchers who developed the instrument. Read the historical section on the 2005 publication of EASE and the section describing the notion of basic or minimal self; those are the passages used in this lesson. Note the perspective: the authors conclude that basic self-disorder is a crucial phenotype, so their summary of the evidence is an argument for a research programme rather than a neutral review. Read its stated limitations and its description of what EASE training involves.

readings.title: Disturbance of Minimal Self (Ipseity) in Schizophrenia: Clarification and Current Status — PMC3984529
readings.note: Read this for the critical side: the two proposed levels of experiential self, the open questions the authors list about specificity, internal structure and pathogenesis, the observation that related metacognitive and narrative-self deficits are found in borderline personality disorder, and the remark that comparisons with other psychoses had not been made. Useful as a contrast to the review above; reading the two together is the point of the lesson.

readings.title: Nordgaard, J. & Parnas, J. (2014), 'Self-disorders and the Schizophrenia Spectrum: A Study of 100 First Hospital Admissions', Schizophrenia Bulletin 40(6):1300-1307 — PMC4193705
readings.note: Read the Methods to see what 'self-disorders aggregate in the spectrum' was compared against, and the Results and Conclusions for the single-factor solution, the high internal consistency, the moderate correlations, and the absence of a difference between schizophrenia and schizotypal disorders. This is the study behind the lesson's group-level claims.

readings.title: Nelson, B. et al. (2012), 'Basic Self-Disturbance Predicts Psychosis Onset in the Ultra High Risk for Psychosis Prodromal Population', Schizophrenia Bulletin 38(6):1277-1287 — PMC3494062
readings.note: Read the sample size (49 ultra-high-risk participants, 52 controls), the mean follow-up of about 569 days, the Cox regression result and the exploratory analysis of spectrum cases. Note the Discussion's own framing: 'closing in' on risk, and its acknowledgement that basic self-disturbance findings require further work. The lesson uses this study as an example of promising but small-sample prospective evidence.

visual.title: Five labelled links from description to clinical promise, each with its failure point
visual.description: A chain diagram showing how a phenomenological concept becomes a measured construct and then a clinical claim, with the specific thing that can go wrong at each link.
steps: Link 1 — Description: a clinician writes that a person's thoughts feel 'spoken by someone else' but still located in the head. Failure point: the wording is unique to one clinician and cannot be recognised by another.

Link 2 — Coding scheme: anchor examples are written so a trained rater can decide whether a reported experience instantiates the anomaly; EASE is published in 2005. Failure point: the item captures only what a trained interviewer can elicit and recognise, so concealment or difficulty in describing produces false negatives.

Link 3 — Group comparison: scores are compared across diagnostic groups; in 100 first admissions, self-disorders aggregate in the schizophrenia spectrum with a one-factor structure and excellent internal consistency. Failure point: groups were formed by the categories the construct is later said to characterise, so boundary choices leak into the result.

Link 4 — Prospective prediction: 49 ultra-high-risk participants followed for about 569 days; total score predicts time to transition with other predictors controlled. Failure point: small sample, one cohort, interview-defined outcome, no threshold or predictive values reported.

Link 5 — Clinical promise: 'the core vulnerability of schizophrenia, measurable at intake'. Failure point: the jump from group association to individual decision needs base rates and validation in the local population, which no study in the chain supplies; the field's own critical literature also reports unresolved specificity.

lessons.title: What a measurement scale claims: reliability, validity, invariance and meaningful change
lessons.explanation:
A score is not a fact; it is a claim, and a claim can be broken into parts that are separately testable. This lesson separates those parts, using depression and anxiety scales as the worked examples because they are the most widely used instruments in the field. Education only: no instrument described here is being recommended for any person, and none of this is advice about treatment.

The COnsensus-based Standards for the selection of health Measurement INstruments project (COSMIN) exists because of confusion about exactly this. Its own account records that the steering committee, founded in 2005, was inspired by a lack of clarity in the literature about terminology and definitions of measurement properties, and that there are many instruments measuring the same construct, so researchers and clinicians must choose [1]. COSMIN's contribution is a taxonomy: reliability, measurement error, validity (content, construct, criterion), responsiveness and interpretability, each with a definition that says what evidence is needed [1].

Four questions follow, and they are not the same question.

Does the instrument give the same answer twice? This is reliability, and its weaker cousin internal consistency asks whether items covary. Internal consistency is the statistic most often reported and the least informative on its own: eleven items about feeling low will hang together whether or not they measure depression rather than, say, distress in general. A scale can be highly reliable and measure the wrong construct consistently.

Does it measure the intended construct and relate to other things as theory predicts? This is construct validity, and it is not established by a single study or a single coefficient. Content validity — whether the items cover the construct as clinicians and patients understand it — is a judgement supported by evidence about item generation and cognitive interviewing, not by a correlation.

Does the same number mean the same thing in different groups? This is measurement invariance, and it has to be tested rather than assumed, because a scale developed in one language and population can behave differently in another. A study of the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 in four large nationally representative European samples found the scores to be unidimensional, reliable and largely free of differential item functioning, while some countries had higher latent variable means than the UK and Ireland, with no evidence of differential item functioning [2]. Read that sentence slowly: 'higher means' is a substantive finding about distress levels, and it is only interpretable as such because item functioning was checked first. Without that check, a country difference could be an artefact of how an item reads in another language.

How much change matters? This is interpretability, and it has no universal answer. A longitudinal study in UK primary care estimated the change thresholds at which people were more likely to report improvement on a global rating, stratified by baseline severity, and found threshold scores of -1.7 points on the PHQ-9, -3.5 on the BDI-II and -1.5 on the GAD-7 for moderate baseline severity; it also found that patients with milder symptoms required much larger reductions as a percentage of their baseline to endorse improvement, and it concluded that an MCID representing a 20% reduction of scores is a useful guide for patients with moderately severe symptoms [3]. A separate study estimating the minimally important difference for the four fixed-length PROMIS depression scales, using data from three randomised trials in adults with chronic pain or prior stroke and mild-to-moderate depression severity, concluded that a T-score of 3 to 4 points is reasonable [4]. Two credible papers, two different scales, two different numbers — which is the point. There is no five-point rule that travels.

One more distinction belongs here because it is routinely muddled. A minimal detectable change is about the noise floor of an instrument: if the measurement error is large relative to the effect being claimed, a change score may be indistinguishable from measurement noise. Illustrative arithmetic, not a property of any named scale: with a standard error of measurement of 2.0 points, a 95% threshold for change beyond noise is 1.96 x sqrt(2) x 2.0 = 5.5 points, and an 80% threshold is 3.6 points. A trial or a clinic reporting a 2-point improvement on such an instrument is operating inside the noise; the same 2-point change on an instrument with a standard error of 0.5 is a different claim entirely. Neither statistic tells you whether the change mattered to the person, which is what an anchor-based minimally important difference tries to capture — and which inherits the noisiness of the global rating used as the anchor.
lessons.example:
A fictional quality-improvement scenario, chosen because it is where scale misuse does the most damage.

A community mental health team adopts the PHQ-9 for everyone on its caseload, reports mean scores monthly, and announces a target of a 5-point reduction per patient per quarter. A new clinician raises three objections, and this is how each one resolves.

Objection one: some patients cannot use the scale as intended. Resolution: valid. Among the PHQ-9's nine items, the scoring convention includes a tenth functional-impairment item that is not part of the total; a service reporting 'the score' has to say which number it means. More importantly, the instrument assumes the person reports symptoms about the last two weeks in a comparable way. That assumption is documented as tested in the psychometric literature for some populations [2] and untested for others; a service using it in a language and literacy context where invariance has not been examined is making an assumption, not a measurement.

Objection two: 5 points is arbitrary. Resolution: substantially valid. The primary-care study's estimated thresholds for people with moderate baseline severity were considerably smaller than 5 points, and its authors' own guidance was a 20% reduction for patients with moderately severe symptoms [3]; a fixed 5-point target across all severity levels also creates a predictable artefact, because people with mild baseline scores cannot lose 5 points without becoming asymptomatic, and people with the highest scores have the most room for regression to the mean to look like improvement. For a score of 15, a 20% reduction is {pct20} points — the same arithmetic, applied to the person's own baseline rather than a target imposed on the caseload.

Objection three: the measure might improve without the person improving. Resolution: valid and important. A global rating of improvement has to come from somewhere; the primary-care study used a self-reported global rating of change as the anchor, which is a person's own judgement and therefore closer to what matters than a coefficient, but also subject to its own recall and framing effects [3]. A service that reports average score change as its outcome has not established that patients got better, only that numbers moved — and it has created an incentive to focus effort where scores can move.

The constructive end point: use the instrument for conversation and for change over time within a person, choose a threshold defensible in the source literature for that severity band, and keep at least one outcome that the person defines. That combination is the least bad option currently available; nothing in this lesson claims it solves measurement in psychiatry.
lessons.question: A trainee reports: 'The team uses a well-validated depression scale, so our mean score is a valid measurement of depression severity in our population.' Which correction is best supported by this lesson's sources?
lessons.answer: Validity is specific to the population, language and use; a scale with good psychometric evidence elsewhere still needs invariance and interpretability evidence in the population being measured, so the mean score is a measurement claim rather than a fact.
lessons.distractor: A scale's validity is established once by its validation studies and then applies wherever the scale is used, so the trainee's statement is correct as long as the version in use is the validated version.
lessons.correction: The trainee's statement assumes the psychometric properties travel with the instrument. The invariance study exists precisely because they may not: it tested item functioning across four national samples before interpreting cross-country differences in latent means [2], and the fact that it found the scales largely free of differential item functioning is an empirical result, not a guarantee that applies to the next language and population. Reliability and validity are also different properties, and COSMIN's taxonomy separates them for that reason [1]. Finally, 'valid measurement of severity' still leaves open what the number means and how much change matters, which requires an anchor-based threshold for that instrument and severity band [3][4].

depth.definitions:
Reliability: the consistency of scores across repeated measurements or raters. Internal consistency: the degree to which items in a scale correlate with one another; a necessary but far from sufficient property. Measurement error: the part of a score that is not signal; COSMIN lists it as a distinct measurement property from reliability [1]. Construct validity: the extent to which an instrument measures the construct it is intended to measure, supported by a network of hypotheses and evidence. Content validity: whether the items adequately cover the construct, judged with evidence about how items were generated and understood. Criterion validity: agreement with a gold standard, awkward in psychiatry because the standard is often another clinical judgement. Measurement invariance: whether the instrument functions equivalently across groups (language, country, gender, diagnostic group); differential item functioning (DIF) is a specific violation in which an item behaves differently for equal underlying severity. Interpretability: what a score and a change in a score mean. MCID (minimal clinically important difference) and MID (minimally important difference): anchor-based estimates of the smallest change a person would consider important. Minimal detectable change (MDC): a threshold derived from measurement error beyond which a change is unlikely to be noise.

Prerequisite: lesson 65 for instruments in clinical use and the arithmetic of predictive value; lesson 73's material on base rates is used in lessons 76-77.
depth.mechanism:
Why do these properties dissociate? Because each answers a different counterfactual.

Reliability asks: if nothing changed, would the score change? Its enemies are task-irrelevant variance — moment-to-moment fluctuation in symptoms, variation in how an item is read, interviewer effects. Internal consistency partly controls the last of these by adding items and averaging, which is why longer scales tend to look better behaved, and why scale length is a silent confounder in comparisons between instruments.

Validity asks: is the variance the score tracks the variance we care about? Here is the crux — reliability is a precondition for validity, not a form of it. A scale measuring the consistency of the room's temperature would be reliable, and useless for depression. Studies reporting only internal consistency have reported only the floor.

Invariance asks: does the same latent level produce the same observed score in this group? The mechanism of violation is ordinary: an item translated as 'feeling bad about yourself' may be read in one context as moral self-criticism and in another as a general judgement about one's circumstances. If large numbers of people in the comparison group read it differently, then a difference in means is partly a difference in reading. Testing invariance — configural, metric, scalar — is machinery for checking this in order, and the four-country study reports the result of that process for PHQ-9 and GAD-7 [2].

Interpretability asks: how much change is enough? Two families of method compete. Distribution-based methods use the standard error and the spread of scores (this is where MDC lives). Anchor-based methods use an external judgement of change, usually the patient's own global rating. Anchor-based estimates are more clinically meaningful and less mathematically clean: the anchor is itself a measurement, with error, and different anchors give different values. The primary-care estimates used a global rating of change stratified by baseline severity, which is why the resulting thresholds are severity-specific and why the authors' summary was a percentage reduction rule rather than one number [3]. Any service that adopts a single number across all severities has removed the severity stratification the source kept.
depth.secondExample:
A contrasting case where the measuring instrument is the clinician rather than a questionnaire, which exposes a different set of failure modes.

Suppose a service decides to audit the quality of its diagnostic assessments by asking two senior clinicians to rate each new note on a five-point 'adequacy' scale. The service reports high agreement between the raters and concludes that the audit is sound. Reason through it.

What has been established: inter-rater consistency on this scale for this pair of raters on these notes. What has not: whether the scale measures adequacy rather than length, seniority-mimicry, or agreement with the raters' own style. Consistent with the COSMIN taxonomy's separation of reliability from validity [1], the audit has produced a reliability result and no validity result at all. The equivalent of invariance is also missing: the two raters share a training background, so their agreement tells us nothing about whether a clinician from another background would rate the same notes the same way. In the psychometric literature this is precisely the problem that motivated formal invariance testing rather than inspection [2].

Then the interpretability question, which is where such audits usually fail hardest. Is one point of 'adequacy' meaningful? There is no anchor. The lesson from the depression-scale literature is that the answer requires a reference point outside the scale — a global rating, a clinical outcome, or a subsequent event — and that different reference points give different answers, which is why the published thresholds are banded by severity and reported as ranges and rules rather than constants [3][4].

Transferable comparison: patient-reported scales fail because people interpret items differently and because change thresholds are contested; clinician-rated scales fail because the variability being averaged is the clinicians' own judgement, and the anchor for 'good enough' is usually another clinician's opinion. Both are measurable, both are fallible, and neither improves by being called objective.
depth.mistake:
The most common misconception, and the one that costs the most, is that a high coefficient means a good instrument. Alpha of 0.'9' tells you the items covary; it does not tell you they covary about the construct you want, and adding near-duplicate items raises it. The corresponding error in reading papers is to accept 'the scale showed good reliability' as the psychometric section.

The second misconception is that validation is a property of the instrument that can be inherited from a validation paper. COSMIN's own framing is that researchers and clinicians must choose among many instruments for the same construct, which requires reviewing the evidence for measurement properties rather than looking up whether a scale is 'validated' [1]. The invariance study shows what checking looks like when it is done properly and what it delivers: a finding about latent means that is interpretable only after item functioning was tested [2].

The third is the concrete confusion between clinical importance and statistical significance, usually in the form of treating any statistically significant change as important. Two papers give different minimal-change estimates for different instruments, severities and populations — -1.7 PHQ-9 points at moderate severity in primary care [3]; 3-4 T-score points for PROMIS depression in trial samples with chronic pain or stroke and mild-to-moderate severity [4] — and neither supports a universal threshold. Diagnostic correction: when someone quotes a minimal important difference, ask for the instrument, the population, the anchor and the baseline severity band. If any of the four is missing, the number is being used as a slogan.
depth.application:
Nonblocking task. A fictional clinic proposes to measure outcomes with a six-item distress scale previously validated in outpatient oncology, in a population of adults with severe mental illness and limited literacy. Before adopting it, write a 200-word plan answering four questions: which measurement property evidence you would require; which piece of evidence a validation study in another population cannot provide; what you would use as an anchor to decide how much change matters; and one alternative or complement you would keep alongside it.

Model response. Property evidence required: content validity evidence for this population (how the items were generated and understood, ideally with cognitive interviews), structural validity and internal consistency, test-retest reliability in this population, and responsiveness, i.e. evidence that the scale changes when the construct changes [1]. What a validation study in another population cannot provide: invariance. Item functioning may differ by literacy level, language and symptom profile, and cross-group mean comparisons are uninterpretable before that is checked — the four-country PHQ-9 study exists to demonstrate both the test and how much can be learned from it [2]. Anchor: a patient-defined rating of what changed and whether it mattered, elicited in the person's own words, used to interpret score changes rather than to generate them; the primary-care MCID study's approach of stratifying by baseline severity is the model, and the number it produced for a different scale in a different population is not transferable [3]. Complement: a functional or goal-based measure counted separately, and the record of the person's own stated goal, so that improvement has a referent other than the scale summary.

Rubric: 1 point for separating reliability from validity explicitly; 1 for naming invariance rather than 'cultural adaptation' in general terms; 1 for an anchor that comes from the person rather than from the distribution of scores; 1 for proposing a complementary measure and saying why. Three or four points indicates the properties are being kept apart; two or fewer usually means 'validated' is still being treated as a property of the instrument.
depth.summary:
Measurement in psychiatry is a set of separately testable claims: consistency (does it repeat?), internal structure (do items cohere?), construct and content validity (does it measure the target?), invariance (does it behave the same across groups?), and interpretability (what does the number, and a change in it, mean?) [1]. No single coefficient answers more than one of these, and the published record shows each question being answered carefully at least somewhere: unidimensional, largely DIF-free PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scores with interpretable cross-country mean differences [2]; severity-stratified minimal-change thresholds from primary care [3]; a different minimal-change estimate for a different instrument in a different population [4].

Transfer: this is the vocabulary you need for the rest of the level. Unit 2's critique of treatment evidence turns on whether trial outcomes were meaningful to begin with, whether trial scales behaved equivalently across arms, and whether a mean change exceeded instrument noise — all of which are the properties defined here. The next lesson stays with the categories themselves: what happens when the boundary of a diagnosis moves, who moves it, and what evidence is used.

readings.title: COSMIN initiative description: 'The COnsensus-based Standards for the selection of health Measurement INstruments (COSMIN) and how to select an outcome measurement instrument' — PMC4900032
readings.note: Read the introduction (why the terminology problem motivated COSMIN) and the passage listing the measurement properties with their definitions. This is the source for the lesson's insistence that reliability, measurement error, validity and responsiveness are distinct claims. The paper is programmatic: it is arguing for standardisation, so its own account of the field's confusion is part of its case rather than a neutral history.

readings.title: Measurement invariance of the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) and Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale (GAD-7) across four European countries (BMC Psychiatry 2022) — PMC8886334
readings.note: Read the Methods for what invariance testing involves (dimensionality, reliability, differential item functioning) and the Results and Conclusions for the findings used here: unidimensional and reliable scores, largely free of differential item functioning, with higher latent means in some countries. Use it to see why a cross-group mean difference requires this check before it can be read as a difference in distress.

readings.title: Kounali, D. et al. (2020), 'How much change is enough? Evidence from a longitudinal study on depression in UK primary care', Psychological Medicine, doi:10.1017/S0033291720003700 (author copy via UCL Discovery)
readings.note: Read the abstract for the estimated thresholds used here (-1.7 PHQ-9, -3.5 BDI-II, -1.5 GAD-7 at moderate baseline severity) and the conclusion about a 20% reduction for moderately severe symptoms; then read the methods to see that the anchor was a self-reported global rating of change stratified by baseline severity, and check the limitations section. Access note: this link is the author's accepted manuscript in a university repository; the version of record is behind the journal, so page numbers differ.

readings.title: Kroenke, K. et al. (2020), 'Minimally Important Differences and Severity Thresholds are Estimated for the PROMIS Depression Scales from Three Randomized Clinical Trials', Journal of Affective Disorders 266:100-108 — PMC7103541
readings.note: Read the methods for the trial samples and the conclusions for the MID estimate (a T-score of 3 to 4 points). The value should be read as instrument-, anchor- and population-specific: three trials in adults with chronic pain or previous stroke and mild-to-moderate depression. Comparing this number with the primary-care thresholds used above is the exercise.

visual.title: Ladder of five questions, from 'does it repeat?' to 'does this change matter?'
visual.description: A labelled ladder in which each rung is a distinct measurement property, its typical statistic, and the specific error made by treating it as proof of the rung above.
steps: Rung 1 — Consistency: does the score repeat when nothing changed? Evidence: test-retest correlation, inter-rater agreement. Error: reading a high coefficient as evidence that the scale measures the right construct.
Rung 2 — Internal structure: do the items behave as one coherent thing? Evidence: internal consistency, factor analysis. Error: adding near-duplicate items to raise alpha, and reporting only alpha.

Rung 3 — Validity: does the score track the construct, including its content as clinicians and patients understand it? Evidence: convergent and discriminant relations, item generation and cognitive interviewing. Error: assuming content validity because the items look sensible to the authors.

Rung 4 — Invariance: does the same underlying severity produce the same score across groups? Evidence: multi-group tests and differential item functioning. Error: interpreting a cross-country mean difference before item functioning has been checked.

Rung 5 — Interpretability: how much change matters, and is a claimed change above the noise floor? Evidence: severity-stratified anchor-based thresholds; standard error of measurement. Error: applying one number from one instrument and population to every patient and every service target.

lessons.title: How a category changes: boundary revision, evidence and interests
lessons.explanation:
Lessons 35 and 68 described what a manual's criteria specify and where the line between distress and disorder is drawn. This lesson asks a different question: when the line moves, what moved it? Education only; nothing here diagnoses anyone, and no guidance about anyone's care is offered.

Start with the programme that gave modern criteria their ambition. In 1970, Eli Robins and Samuel Guze published 'Establishment of diagnostic validity in psychiatric illness: its application to schizophrenia' in the American Journal of Psychiatry [1]. Its premise was that a psychiatric diagnosis should earn validity the way a medical diagnosis does, through a specified research programme rather than by expert assertion, and its immediate practical descendant was the set of research criteria published from Washington University in 1972, which Kenneth Kendler describes as the basis from which Spitzer, Endicott and Robins developed the Research Diagnostic Criteria [2]. The word that does the work in this programme is validator: an external fact — course of illness, family aggregation, treatment response, laboratory finding — against which a proposed category can be tested.

Kendler's historical essay makes the stakes of that word explicit. He notes that different authors emphasised different validators, so that experts using distinct essential criteria produced incompatible classifications, and he compares the resulting confusion to the parallel confusion in early zoological taxonomy: initial attempts at species definition used top-down approaches based on a few essential features chosen a priori by experts, an approach later rejected and replaced by bottom-up approaches using a much wider array of features [2]. His normative conclusion is worth writing down: since we cannot assume that our categories carve nature at its joints, the only way to make progress is to require that each periodic revision contains improvements on its predecessor — changes made only on the basis of convincing evidence that, using an agreed-upon set of validators, the new criteria outperform the old [2]. Read that as a quality-control proposal, and then check whether real revisions met it.

Case one: a category removed. Drescher's account of the depathologising of homosexuality records that in 1973 the American Psychiatric Association removed the diagnosis of homosexuality from the second edition of the DSM, after competing theories — those that regarded it as a disorder and those that did not — were compared, and it documents the continuing argument, including the objection that if homosexuality were a disorder because it caused distress, then other characteristics that cause distress would also qualify; the residual category of ego-dystonic homosexuality was removed in the next revision, DSM-III-R, in 1987 [3]. Two things follow for our purposes. First, the revision was not a single decisive study: it was a contest among theories and evidence in which social and professional pressures were visibly part of the history, which the article's closing section on the sociocultural aftermath makes plain [3]. Second, the removal happened in stages, with a residual category surviving fourteen years — the ordinary texture of boundary change.

Case two: the reliability standard itself moving. The DSM-5 field trials produced lower kappa reliability estimates than earlier trials, and the argument about what they meant turned on method and on thresholds. An independent study that diagnosed patients twice — using the same interview for both — reported a mean kappa of 0.80 using the audio-recording method and 0.47 using the test-retest method, with about a quarter of the test-retest estimates classed as poor, and described how members of the DSM-5 Task Force, using revised kappa guidelines, interpreted the field-trial results as indicating good to very good reliability for most diagnoses while critics argued the manual had failed its reliability tests under traditional guidelines; the same paper notes that many instruments of this kind record agreement only from the sample at hand, and that in one year of articles reporting diagnostic data on specific DSM categories, only a minority reported sample-derived kappa estimates at all [4].

Case three: a design change with measurable effect. The ICD-11 developmental field study assessed inter-diagnostician reliability for high-burden mental disorders in 13 countries, weighted kappas ranged from 0.45 for dysthymic disorder to 0.88 for social anxiety disorder — moderate to almost perfect by the standards used — and the authors report that reliability for the ICD-11 diagnostic guidelines was superior to that previously reported for the equivalent ICD-10 guidelines [5]. Guidelines can be written to be used more consistently; that is a real achievement and it is also, strictly, an achievement on the reliability axis, not the validity axis.

The synthesis, and where the honest uncertainty sits. Categories in psychiatry are revisable instruments, not discoveries with expiry dates: they are changed by committees on the basis of agreed validators, contested evidence, practical consequences and, at least sometimes, social pressure. Reliability can be improved by design; validity does not follow from reliability. And the difference between criteria and judgement survives all of this: a criteria set specifies conditions that a case may meet, while clinical judgement is the business of deciding what is going on with this person, including the possibility that the criteria are a poor fit — the subject lesson 35 opened and lesson 80 will close.
lessons.example:
Worked reasoning on a revision question, using a fictional-sounding but realistic scenario: a service encounters an increase in recorded diagnoses after a manual change, and wants to know what changed.

The change: a former exclusion rule is relaxed, so that a syndrome may be diagnosed during a period of bereavement or another defined circumstance. Recorded rates rise. Two explanations compete. Explanation A: the change detected a group of people who were previously under-recognised, so the increase is truth. Explanation B: the change moved the threshold, so the additional cases are people whose presentation would formerly have been recorded as normal-range responses to loss, and the increase is partly reclassification.

What would distinguish them? Not the mere fact of more diagnoses — both explanations predict that. Discriminating evidence would be a validator that behaves differently between the newly captured group and the previously defined group: a course-of-illness difference (do the new cases persist?), a family-aggregation difference (do relatives show the same pattern more often?), a treatment-response difference, or a difference on a biological or psychological measure. This is the discipline Robins and Guze's programme sets [1], and Kendler's requirement sharpens it: a revision should be justified by evidence that the new criteria improve on the predecessor under an agreed set of validators [2]. Absent such evidence, the increase is a description of the criteria, not of the world.

Now the reliability wrinkle. Suppose the newly captured cases also produce increased variability between clinicians, because the boundary now requires a judgement about the severity of grief. Then field-trial-style reliability estimates for that diagnosis could fall even though the criteria changed for good reasons — precisely the pattern observed when a longstanding diagnosis's kappa dropped in the DSM-5 field trials and commentators divided over whether the criteria, the method or the thresholds were at fault [4]. Note the form of that disagreement: everyone accepted the numbers and disputed the interpretation, which is what competent disagreement about measurement looks like.

Finally, consider the competing costs, because boundary changes are not free in either direction. A criterion that is too strict turns people away from recognition and from services that require a diagnosis; a criterion that is too loose medicalises ordinary experience and can attach a label that follows a person. Neither the psychiatric literature nor any manual resolves that trade-off, because it is a question about values and about what a society wants a diagnosis to do. The lesson's claim is narrower and firmer: whoever claims a boundary change was justified owes you the validator, the comparison and the group that was affected.
lessons.question: A trainee writes: 'The ICD-11 field study showed kappas from 0.45 to 0.88 with better reliability than ICD-10, so the ICD-11 categories are more valid than the ICD-10 ones.' What is the precise error?
lessons.answer: The finding concerns inter-diagnostician agreement; better agreement is a reliability result and does not establish validity, which still requires evidence from validators such as course, family aggregation or treatment response.
lessons.distractor: There is no error: reliability is the main evidence for validity in psychiatric classification, so improved kappa values are the strongest available support for a manual's categories.
lessons.correction: The study's own outcome is inter-diagnostician reliability for 13 countries, with weighted kappas from 0.45 to 0.88, and its conclusion concerns the suitability of the guidelines for implementation [5]. Improving agreement is a genuine advance: it means two clinicians given the same guidelines more often arrive at the same label, which is a precondition for research and for consistent service communication. But agreement between clinicians can be high and the category still poor at picking out a coherent illness; Kendler's argument requires that a revision be shown to improve on its predecessor under an agreed set of validators, which reliability statistics alone cannot show [2]. A better version of the trainee's sentence would be: 'ICD-11 guidelines achieved better agreement than ICD-10 guidelines, which is a reliability result; whether the categories are more valid is a separate question that this study does not address.'

depth.definitions:
Validator: an external source of evidence used to test whether a proposed diagnostic category is a coherent entity — canonical examples include characteristic course, family aggregation, response to treatment, and biological or psychological correlates. The concept is used in this sense in the nosological literature [2]. Reliability: agreement or reproducibility of judgements, whether between clinicians at one time or in the same person over time; kappa is the standard chance-corrected statistic and comes in several variants, which matters when comparing studies. Test-retest versus inter-rater designs: whether the same or different clinicians repeat the assessment, and how the second assessment is conducted, change the estimate substantially [4]. Field trial: a study run before or alongside the publication of a classification to estimate its reliability and usability in ordinary practice [4]. Revision: the scheduled process by which a manual's criteria are changed; in the DSM and ICD systems these are committee processes with drafted criteria, field testing, review and publication [2][5]. Diagnosticity: how well a category picks out a group with something in common beyond the criteria themselves.

Prerequisite: lesson 35 for what criteria specify and cannot settle; lesson 68 for the threshold between distress and disorder and the dimensionality critique; lesson 31 for the four levels of description.
depth.mechanism:
Why do boundaries move, and why is movement so hard to adjudicate? Four mechanisms operate at once.

First, validators are not all available or equally weighted. A follow-up study requires decades; a family study requires cooperation from relatives; a treatment-response validator is contaminated by the fact that treatments are not specific; laboratory validators in psychiatry are mostly absent. Kendler's account of nineteenth-century nosology shows what happens when the choice of validator is left to individual experts: different authors emphasise different validators and produce incompatible classifications [2]. The modern criteria-based approach is an attempt to fix this by agreeing on validators in advance — which trades one problem (incommensurable schemes) for another (an agreed metric that may not capture what matters).

Second, reliability and validity interact asymmetrically. Better reliability makes validity research possible, because a measure that disagrees with itself cannot be correlated with anything reliably. But reliability can be raised in ways that suppress validity, most obviously by narrowing criteria until only unambiguous cases qualify, which produces tidy agreement about an unrepresentative group. The ICD-11 field study's improvement over ICD-10 [5] and the dispute over the DSM-5 field trials' lower kappas [4] are two faces of the same issue: what the numbers mean depends on what the assessment procedure asked clinicians to do.

Third, the method used to estimate reliability is itself a choice. In the study cited above, the audio-recording approach to a repeat diagnosis produced a mean kappa of 0.80 while the test-retest approach produced 0.47 in the same overall programme, with about a quarter of test-retest estimates classed as poor [4]. If a manual's official reliability can differ by more than 0.3 depending on whether the second assessment is a recording review or a fresh interview, then a headline claim that a manual is or is not reliable is under-specified. This is the same lesson as lesson 73's invariance point, applied to categories instead of scales.

Fourth, non-evidential forces are real and should be named without being treated as decisive. The removal of homosexuality from DSM-II in 1973 involved theoretical competition and visible social and professional pressure, and the removal was completed in stages, with ego-dystonic homosexuality surviving until DSM-III-R in 1987 [3]. Naming those forces is not the same as saying the outcome was wrong; it is refusing to tell a story in which evidence alone decided.
depth.secondExample:
A contrasting case where a boundary is drawn not by a manual but by a service, which shows that revision is an everyday act, not a rare historical one.

A fictional community team decides which referrals to accept, using unwritten criteria: 'we take people who are unwell enough to need us'. Over two years, its recorded caseload changes composition. Meanwhile, a neighbouring team defines its threshold in writing, using a specific functional-impairment criterion, and its recorded caseload looks different.

Now apply the lesson's machinery. Both teams have 'categories'; only one has published criteria. The written threshold is testable in a way the unwritten one is not: another clinician can check whether a given referral meets it, which allows agreement to be estimated, and the team can ask what the threshold picks out. The unwritten threshold has perfect local validity in the sense that whoever applies it thinks it is right, and no reliability at all across people or across time — the exact pathology that motivated the move to operational criteria in the first place, and that Kendler's history describes as ending in incompatible schemata [2].

Next, apply the validator test that the lesson's main example used. If the team wants to claim that its threshold identifies people who need the service, it needs evidence that the group above the threshold does better, or differs in course, from those below it — the same requirement Robins and Guze's programme imposes on a diagnosis [1]. Almost no service can produce that evidence, which is why service thresholds tend to be defended by waiting lists and incident reviews instead. That is not cynicism about the teams; it is a statement about what the evidence would need to look like.

The transferable comparison: manual revision and service gatekeeping differ in visibility and in scope, not in kind. Both draw lines, both must accept that the line can be wrong, and both can be assessed by asking what the line picks out, how consistently it is applied, and what happens to the people on either side.
depth.mistake:
Misconception one: that a change to the manual reflects a new discovery about nature. Sometimes it does; often it reflects a decision about where to put a threshold, what to exclude, or what language to use. The homosexuality case is the clearest available demonstration that categories can be removed as the surrounding theory and the surrounding society change, and that the process takes years and leaves residues [3].

Misconception two: that reliability is the same as validity, in the specific form of reading a kappa as a warrant. The ICD-11 field study is a reliability study and its authors frame it that way [5]; the DSM-5 controversy was largely a debate about which reliability threshold to apply and which method to use [4]. Neither resolves whether the categories carve out coherent illness.

Misconception three: that criteria and clinical judgement are rivals, so that a good clinician 'sees through' the manual or a rigorous one 'follows' it. The working relationship is different: criteria standardise the description of a case for comparison and communication; judgement concerns whether the description is a good fit for this person, what else might explain the presentation, and what the person wants. Kendler's framing — improvements must be demonstrated against agreed validators — implies that the manual is an instrument under warranty review, not a verdict delivered per case [2]. Practical correction: in a note, quote the criteria that were met, then state the judgement and its basis separately; a reader who cannot tell the two apart cannot disagree with either.
depth.application:
Nonblocking task. Take the fictional headline: 'New study finds that a proposed diagnosis captures a distinct group; researchers call for it to be added to the next revision of the manual.' The study reported: 212 patients meeting the proposed criteria; high internal consistency of the symptom checklist; 71% had another diagnosis removed after assessment; follow-up of 9 months showed 64% still met criteria.

Write a 150-word appraisal with four labelled sentences: what the study does establish; which validator is missing that a revision committee would expect; one alternative explanation for the 71% figure; and what you would need before supporting the addition.

Model response. Establishes: that the proposed criteria can be applied to a sample and are internally consistent, and that the presentation is not wholly transient over nine months in two-thirds of cases. Missing validator: comparison against a predecessor category or against an alternative grouping under an agreed validator — a family-aggregation study, a course-of-illness difference from neighbouring conditions, or a treatment-response difference — which is what Kendler's standard requires of a revision [2], and which the history of the field's validation programme treats as the point of the exercise [1]. Alternative explanation for 71%: diagnostic substitution, in which assessors applying new criteria to people who previously received a neighbouring diagnosis record the new label instead; this is a bookkeeping change rather than a discovery, and it would produce exactly this figure without any difference in the patients. What I would need: a head-to-head comparison of the proposed criteria and the incumbent under a validator agreed in advance, in a sample large enough to estimate agreement and outcome rates; plus a report of how many people were reclassified in each direction and what happened to them.

Rubric: 1 point for correctly identifying that internal consistency is not a validator; 1 for naming at least one validator that requires comparison rather than description; 1 for the substitution explanation or another mechanism that explains the numbers without new discovery; 1 for requiring a comparison rather than more samples of the same design. Three or four points indicates the difference between describing a category and validating it; two or fewer indicates that an internally consistent new label is being treated as a discovery.
depth.summary:
Psychiatric categories are revisable instruments. Their modern ambition — validation through agreed external validators rather than expert assertion — dates to the Robins and Guze programme [1] and is stated most sharply in Kendler's argument that revisions should be justified only by evidence that the new criteria improve on their predecessors under an agreed set of validators [2]. Real revisions complicate that story: a category can be removed through a contest of theories and social pressures and survive in residual form for fourteen years [3]; reliability estimates for one manual can differ substantially by method and threshold, and the disagreement can be about interpretation rather than data [4]; and a revision of guidelines can demonstrably improve agreement without settling anything about validity [5].

Transfer: carry three questions to any claim about a diagnosis. What validator was used, and was it agreed in advance? Was reliability the result, validity, or neither? And who is affected by where the line sits? Unit 2 now turns from how categories are made to how the evidence about their treatments is assembled and read, beginning with the fact that a trial reports an average.
