visual.title: Five labelled steps in a category revision, with the evidence each step owes
visual.description: A cycle diagram of how a diagnostic boundary is revised, naming at each step the evidence a reader should look for before accepting the change.
steps: Step 1 — Proposal: a working group drafts or amends criteria. Evidence owed: the stated problem with the incumbent criteria and the reason for the change.

Step 2 — Reliability testing: field trials or field studies estimate agreement using a stated method (audio-recorded review, test-retest, or a fresh interview). Evidence owed: the method, the sample and the agreement statistic, because estimates for the same manual can differ substantially by method.

Step 3 — Validator comparison: the proposed version is compared with the incumbent on agreed external validators such as course, family aggregation or treatment response. Evidence owed: a head-to-head comparison, not more descriptions of the new criteria.

Step 4 — Revision and publication: criteria are changed, sometimes partially, leaving residual categories that may persist for years. Evidence owed: a decision record stating what changed, what did not, and why.

Step 5 — Post-revision consequences: recorded prevalence and reclassification shift; services see different populations. Evidence owed: counts of who moved category and in which direction, so that a bookkeeping shift is not mistaken for a discovery.

lessons.title: The replication problem in psychiatric and psychological research
lessons.explanation:
The previous four lessons established that descriptions, instruments and categories are all fallible constructions. This lesson addresses the same problem at the level of the published literature: the record is a sample, and it is not a random one. Education only.

Begin with vocabulary, because the words are used loosely. A recent review of the field's response to the replicability problem distinguishes replication, the process of repeating a study or experiment with the goal of verifying effects or generalising findings across new models and populations, from reproducibility, assessing the accuracy of research claims based on the original methods, data and code [1]. The distinction matters because the two failures need different remedies: a claim can be reproducible in the narrow sense (the same data and script give the same number) and fail to replicate in a new sample, and it can replicate while being irreproducible because nobody can see how the number was produced.

The most cited statement of the problem is John Ioannidis's 2005 essay. Its framework is analytic rather than empirical: the probability that a research finding is true, he argues, depends on the prior probability that it is true before the study, the statistical power of the study, and the level of statistical significance used, and with increasing bias the chances that a finding is true diminish considerably [2]. His corollaries run in directions that should be familiar from clinical work: smaller studies, smaller effect sizes, greater flexibility in designs and definitions, greater financial interest, and hotter scientific fields all make a claimed finding less likely to be true [2]. Note what kind of claim this is. Ioannidis is not reporting that most psychiatric findings have been measured and found false; he is showing that under plausible assumptions of low prior odds, low power and high flexibility, a majority of significant results would be false. The argument is a proof about probabilities given assumptions, and the assumptions are where it should be argued with — the paper is a diagnostic instrument, not a verdict on any particular field.

The constructive side has a manifesto. Munafò and colleagues argued in Nature Human Behaviour for adopting measures to optimise key elements of the scientific process — methods, reporting and dissemination, reproducibility, evaluation and incentives — and they note that there is some evidence from both simulations and empirical studies supporting the likely effectiveness of these measures, while acknowledging that broad adoption by researchers, institutions, funders and journals will require iterative evaluation and improvement [3]. The hedge is theirs and it belongs in your notes: the remedies are promising and not yet proven at scale.

Now the psychiatry-specific evidence, which is the most useful part of this lesson because it is measured rather than modelled. Scott and Rucklidge examined every clinical trial published between January 2009 and July 2013 in the five psychiatry journals that mandate prospective trial registration. Out of 3305 articles, 181 studies required registration. Of those, 21 (11.6%) were deemed unregistered, 61 (33.7%) were retrospectively registered, 37 (20.4%) had primary outcome measures that were unclear either in the article or in the registry, 2 (1.1%) were registered in a registry the researchers could not access, and only 60 — 33.1% — had been prospectively registered [4].

Sit with the implications of that last figure. Prospective registration is the mechanism that makes outcome switching detectable: without a time-stamped record of what was planned, a reader cannot tell whether an outcome was chosen before or after the data arrived. In journals that required it as a condition of publication, about a third of trials met the standard in that window. This is not evidence that any particular published result is wrong; it is evidence that the design of the literature made it easy for wrong results to survive, and it explains why the next lessons treat published effect sizes as upper bounds rather than measurements.

Two further points of intellectual honesty. First, a failed replication is not automatically a refutation. Replications differ in population, dose, measure, comparator and power, and a null result in a small underpowered study is weak evidence against a real effect, exactly as a positive result in a small study is weak evidence for one. Judging replication requires the same appraisal you would give the original: what was the prior, what was the power, and what would have happened under the alternative. Second, replication failure at the level of mechanism does not decide the clinical question. A study failing to replicate a proposed cognitive or biological mediator says little directly about whether a treatment helps people, because treatments can work for reasons other than the ones proposed by their advocates; conflating the two produces both false scepticism about useful care and false confidence in attractive theories.
lessons.example:
Worked reasoning on a fictional headline, to show how the pieces assemble.

Headline: 'Trial finds a novel therapy cuts relapse by half; researchers call for it to be rolled out.' The paper describes a single-site randomised trial of 84 participants, primary outcome relapse over twelve months, reported as statistically significant with a p value of 0.04. The registry entry, written before recruitment, lists relapse at twelve months as the primary outcome but adds, in a later amendment, a secondary outcome of 'clinical improvement'.

Step one: ask what the claim rests on. One trial, one site, 84 participants, a dichotomous outcome and a p value just under the conventional threshold. From Ioannidis's framework, a single small trial with a modest effect and no strong prior has a substantial chance of producing a false positive under flexible analysis, and small studies are named as one of his corollaries for that reason [2]. This is not a refutation; it is a statement about how much weight the result can bear before replication, particularly if the effect size is large relative to what the literature would predict.

Step two: ask whether the analysis was free to choose. The registry amendment is the key detail. An outcome added after recruitment began is not necessarily illegitimate — trials do add outcomes for good reasons — but it means the reported analyses include at least one choice made with knowledge of the data, which is the flexibility Ioannidis identifies as a driver of false positives [2] and precisely the practice that prospective registration exists to expose [4]. The remedy is ordinary: check whether the primary outcome reported in the paper matches the registry entry, and whether the reported result survives when only pre-specified outcomes are counted.

Step three: ask what a replication would have to look like. Not a repeat of the same design with 84 participants, which would be underpowered to detect the effect it is trying to confirm, but a multi-site trial sized on the effect the first trial found, with the primary outcome fixed in advance, registration before recruitment, and an analysis plan committed to in advance. That is what the manifesto's recommendations amount to when applied to one study [3], and it is why the field's reforms are procedural rather than rhetorical: methods, reporting, reproducibility, evaluation and incentives [3].

Step four, and the one most often skipped: state the decision the evidence currently supports. For a clinician or a commissioner, the honest position after one small positive trial with an amended registry is that the intervention is a research question, not a service option; the position after several adequately powered pre-registered trials pointing the same way is different, even if the individual effect sizes are smaller. The transferable skill is the willingness to describe what you would need to see, rather than choosing between believing and disbelieving.
lessons.question: A reviewer says: 'Replication failure in psychology means most published psychiatric findings are false, so published effect sizes should be treated as meaningless.' What is the best correction?
lessons.answer: The evidence documents specific mechanisms that inflate and distort the published record — incentive structures, flexibility in analysis, and incomplete prospective registration — while the general claim about the proportion of false findings comes from a probability argument with stated assumptions; the appropriate response is to appraise weight of evidence and demand pre-specification, not to treat effect sizes as meaningless.
lessons.distractor: Replication failure is confined to social psychology and has not been documented in psychiatric research, so published effect sizes can be taken at face value.
lessons.correction: The second answer is straightforwardly false: psychiatry has its own measured evidence. In the five psychiatry journals mandating prospective registration, only 60 of 181 trials (33.1%) published between 2009 and 2013 had been prospectively registered, and 61 (33.7%) were registered retrospectively [4]. The first answer is the correction that gets both halves right. Ioannidis's argument is analytic — it shows the probability a finding is true depends on prior odds, power and significance level, and diminishes with bias [2] — so it justifies scepticism proportional to those features rather than blanket dismissal. And 'meaningless' over-corrects in the direction that harms patients, because discarding all effect estimates is not more rigorous than accepting all of them; it simply replaces one unfiltered claim with another. The defensible practice is to weight each claim by its prior plausibility, power, pre-specification and independence, and to prefer replicated effects with consistent direction over dramatic single results.

depth.definitions:
Replication: repeating a study or experiment to verify an effect or to generalise it across new models and populations. Reproducibility: assessing the accuracy of a claim from the original methods, data or code [1]. Researcher degrees of freedom: the set of analytic choices (outcome, subgroup, covariate, stopping rule, exclusion) that a researcher can vary, deliberately or not, and which determine how much a reported result reflects the data rather than the choices. Pre-specification: fixing those choices in advance in a time-stamped registry or protocol. Prospective registration: registering a trial before participants are enrolled, the practice that makes pre-specification checkable [4]. Outcome switching: reporting an outcome different from the registered primary outcome, or promoting a secondary outcome, without disclosure. Publication bias: the tendency for results to be published or reported as a function of their statistical significance, which distorts the summary literature; lesson 77 treats its measurement. Prior odds: the plausibility of a hypothesis before the study, one of Ioannidis's three inputs [2]. Power: the probability of detecting an effect of a given size, if it exists.

Prerequisite: lesson 73 for the distinction between reliability and validity, which reappears here as the difference between reproducing a number and replicating a finding; lesson 65 for the base-rate arithmetic that underlies the prior-odds argument.
depth.mechanism:
Why does a literature distort itself without anyone intending fraud? Four mechanisms, each with the fix that actually addresses it.

Selection on significance. Journals, authors and readers all respond to interesting results, and a significant result is more publishable than a null one from the same study. The consequence is that the published distribution of p values is truncated, which raises the average reported effect size above the true one. The remedy that addresses this at the source is pre-specification plus registered reports, where acceptance depends on the design rather than the outcome.

Flexibility in analysis. With several outcomes, several subgroup definitions, several exclusion rules and several plausible models, there is usually some combination that yields p < 0.05. Because the choice need not be conscious — a researcher can simply notice which way the wind is blowing — the natural correction is not exhortation but committed analysis plans and, where plans change, disclosure of the change and its timing.

Incomplete pre-specification at the level of the record. Even attentive readers cannot detect switching without a registry, which is why the Scott and Rucklidge study matters: it measured how often, in journals that require registration, the requirement was met. Their figures — 11.6% unregistered, 33.7% retrospective, only 33.1% prospective, with a further 20.4% whose primary outcomes were unclear [4] — quantify a structural constraint on what any reader of that literature could have concluded.

Incentives. Careers, funding and reputations reward novel positive findings. Munafò and colleagues treat incentives as one of the elements to be optimised alongside methods and reporting, and their honesty about evidence is worth preserving: they report that there is some evidence from simulations and empirical studies for the likely effectiveness of the proposed measures while stating that broad adoption requires iterative evaluation and improvement [3]. Nobody has run the trial that proves open science fixes science.

One further mechanism is specific to psychiatry and worth naming here. Trial outcomes in this field are often clinician- or self-rated scales, and lesson 73 showed that change on such a scale involves anchors, severity bands and measurement error. Flexibility therefore does not stop at the choice of outcome; it extends to how change is defined and scored, which is another reason to read reported effects as conditional on the definitions used.
depth.secondExample:
A contrasting case from clinical measurement rather than trial reporting, showing that the same replication logic applies where nobody is tempted by a p value.

Suppose a fictional health system introduces a standardised questionnaire kiosk in waiting rooms and, after a year, reports that 'distress scores have fallen by 12% across the service'. Underlying it are three separable claims, each with its own replication requirement. The measurement claim — that the questionnaire measures the same thing in June as in December — is a reliability and invariance question in the sense of lesson 73, and it must be settled before the other two. The sampling claim — that the people completing it are comparable across the year — requires evidence about who responded; a change in the mix of attenders can produce a 12% fall without anyone improving, which is the same selection mechanism that distorts the trial literature [2][4]. The causal claim — that something the service did caused the fall — needs a comparison, and there is none.

Note the parallel with the trial example. In the trial, the distorting mechanism was flexibility in outcomes and incomplete registration; in the service audit, it is flexibility in who counts and no registry at all. The remedies are analogous: fix the measure and the population in advance, publish the plan, and report the denominator. And note the parallel failure mode: the same instinct that makes a service want to report improvement makes a researcher want to report a significant interaction, and neither is corrected by appealing to the reporter's good character. It is corrected by making the choice visible before the data arrive, which is what the registration study's 33.1% figure measures the absence of [4].
depth.mistake:
The most damaging misconception is the moralised one — treating replication problems as a story about dishonest researchers. Some fraud exists, but the documented mechanisms operate through ordinary incentives, invisible flexibility and structural gaps in the record, and a moralised frame has a specific harmful consequence: it encourages readers to evaluate findings by trust in the author rather than by the properties of the study. Prefer the properties: prior plausibility, power, pre-specification, independence of the replication, and transparency of the analysis [2][3].

Misconception two: that replication failure means the effect does not exist. Effects can be context-bound, smaller than estimated, or present only in subgroups defined before the study. A failed replication is evidence that a claim was overstated, which is a statement about the claim, not necessarily about the phenomenon.

Misconception three, in the opposite direction: that replication is a technicality for methodologists and does not affect what a clinician should believe. The registration data make the practical stake concrete — in a five-journal sample, two-thirds of trials did not meet the prospective registration standard their journals required [4] — which means that any summary of that literature inherits uncertainty that cannot be resolved by reading the papers more carefully. Diagnostic correction: when you catch yourself thinking 'this study is well written, so I will believe it', substitute 'this study is well written, so I can now check its prior odds, power, and registration'. When you catch yourself thinking 'the literature is broken, so nothing is knowable', substitute the same sentence, because the checks are exactly what makes some claims trustworthy.
depth.application:
Nonblocking task. Using the registration figures in this lesson, produce a three-sentence quantitative briefing for a fictional journal club, assuming the five-journal sample is representative of psychiatric trials published in that period: (a) how many of 100 such trials would you expect to have unmet prospective registration requirements; (b) of those, how many would be unregistered entirely versus retrospectively registered; (c) one sentence on what that implies for reading pooled effect estimates.

Model response, with the arithmetic shown. Of 100 trials, 33.1 would be expected to meet the prospective registration standard and 66.9 not to. Of the 181 trials in the study, 21 were unregistered (11.6% of 181) and 61 retrospective (33.7%); expressed per 100 trials, that is 11.6 unregistered and 33.7 retrospective, leaving 21.6 per 100 with other registration problems (unclear primary outcomes, inaccessible registry). Implication sentence: because only about a third of trials were verifiably pre-specified, pooled effect estimates from this period should be read as upper bounds carrying unknown amounts of selective reporting, which is a statement about the literature's uncertainty rather than about the truth of any individual finding.

Check the arithmetic yourself: 21/181 = 11.6%, 61/181 = 33.7%, 60/181 = 33.1%, and 11.6 + 33.7 + 33.1 = 78.4, leaving 21.6 points for the 37 unclear-outcome and 2 inaccessible-registry cases (20.4% and 1.1%), which sums to 100% to within rounding.

Rubric: 1 point for converting proportions correctly and showing the division; 1 for distinguishing the unregistered group from the retrospectively registered group, which are different problems; 1 for framing the implication as bounded reliability of pooled estimates rather than as a claim that trials are fraudulent. Three points indicates that a measured finding is being used proportionally; fewer usually means the figures have been turned into a verdict.
depth.summary:
The published record is a sample shaped by selection, flexibility, incomplete pre-specification and incentives. Ioannidis's analytic argument shows why a significant finding can be more likely false than true under unfavourable priors, low power and high flexibility [2]; the field's manifesto proposes remedies and honestly reports that their effectiveness is supported by some evidence and requires iterative evaluation [3]; and the psychiatry-specific measurement shows how much of the record was not pre-specified in practice — 33.1% of trials prospectively registered in journals that required it [4]. Replication and reproducibility are different problems needing different fixes [1].

Transfer to unit 2: this lesson explained why a literature can look stronger than it is. The next five lessons work on the reader's side of that problem: how a trial's average effect relates to a person, how reporting bias and uncertainty are appraised and graded, what the control condition actually does, how service-level conditions shape outcomes, and finally how to assemble all of it into a defensible judgement with the uncertainty written down.

readings.title: 'The replication crisis has led to positive structural, procedural, and community changes' (2024 review) — PMC11290608
readings.note: Read the definitions table and the opening section distinguishing replication from reproducibility, and the survey of procedural changes that followed the credibility revolution. The lesson uses this paper only for the vocabulary and for the claim that reforms are ongoing; it is a commentary on the field rather than a measurement of it.

readings.title: Ioannidis, J. P. A. (2005), 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False', PLoS Medicine 2(8):e124
readings.note: Read the abstract, the section setting out the dependence on prior probability, power and significance level, the treatment of bias, and the corollaries about small studies, small effect sizes, flexibility in design and definitions, financial interest and hot fields. Then read Figure 1 and its caption, which reports the probability that a finding is true as a function of pre-study odds at power 0.20, 0.50 and 0.80. Note that the argument is analytic: it is a probability model with stated assumptions, not a measurement of any field, and the assumptions are the place to argue.

readings.title: Munafò, M. R. et al. (2017), 'A manifesto for reproducible science', Nature Human Behaviour 1:0021 — PMC7610724
readings.note: Read the abstract and the section listing the elements to be optimised (methods, reporting and dissemination, reproducibility, evaluation, incentives), plus the authors' own statement that evidence for the proposed measures comes from simulations and empirical studies and that adoption will require iterative evaluation. The hedge is part of the argument and is quoted in the lesson.

readings.title: Scott, A. & Rucklidge, J. J. (2015), 'Is Mandatory Prospective Trial Registration Working to Prevent Publication of Unregistered Trials and Selective Outcome Reporting? An Observational Study of Five Psychiatry Journals That Mandate Prospective Clinical Trial Registration', PLoS ONE 10(8):e0133718 — PMC4546113
readings.note: Read the abstract's Results for the figures used here: 3305 articles screened, 181 trials identified, 21 (11.6%) unregistered, 61 (33.7%) retrospectively registered, 37 (20.4%) with unclear primary outcomes, 2 (1.1%) in an inaccessible registry, and 60 (33.1%) prospectively registered. Read the Discussion for the authors' own limitations, including the study window (January 2009 to July 2013) and the five-journal scope; later evidence suggests reporting practices have improved since, which the next lesson's material on antidepressant trials illustrates.

visual.title: Five labelled stations on the path from a single study to a trustworthy claim
visual.description: A flow diagram showing where the published record can distort a finding, and the specific mechanism at each station together with the check that addresses it.
steps: Station 1 — Hypothesis: the study rests on prior odds. Check: is the hypothesis plausible before the study, or only in this paper's introduction? Failure if unexamined: an implausible hypothesis needs stronger evidence than a plausible one.

Station 2 — Design and power: the study is sized to detect an effect. Check: what effect size was assumed, and how many outcomes, subgroups and models are available to the analyst? Failure if unchecked: underpowered studies with flexible analyses yield both false positives and exaggerated effect sizes.

Station 3 — Pre-specification: outcomes and analyses are fixed in a time-stamped registry before recruitment. Check: does the published primary outcome match the registry entry, and when were amendments made? Failure if absent: retrospective registration and outcome switching become impossible to distinguish from honest reporting.

Station 4 — Publication: the result enters the literature. Check: how much of the evidence base is missing because results were uninteresting, and does the journal's acceptance depend on the direction of the finding? Failure if unchecked: the published distribution is truncated towards positive results.

Station 5 — Accumulation: independent replications, syntheses and reanalyses converge or diverge. Check: whether replication was pre-registered, adequately powered and independent, and whether the summary model accounts for missing results. Failure avoided: treating a first positive trial as an established effect, or a single failed replication as a refutation.

questions.prompt: A fictional supervisor reads a first-assessment note that says: 'Patient reports feeling detached; endorses low mood; denies plans. Impression: depersonalisation.' The interview transcript shows she said 'my arms move before I decide to move them, and I watch it happen as if it were a video of someone else'. Using lesson 71's method, what is the strongest criticism of the note?
questions.answer: It has replaced a specific description of the mode in which her experience is given — actions experienced as happening before her decision and as observed rather than lived — with a category term, and it does not preserve her wording, so a reader cannot check whether the experience was actually of that kind.
questions.distractor: It is too brief, because a proper note should record the patient's full narrative verbatim before any technical term is used.
questions.correction: Length is not the criterion; preservation and separation are. The note fails twice: her words are gone, and a technical term has been used as though it were a finding. 'Verbally at length' is no correction at all if the added text is the clinician's paraphrase. The repair is to quote the two things she actually described, mark 'impression' as an inference with its basis, and state what remains undecided — for instance whether she experiences these episodes as frightening or as neutral, which the record does not say.

questions.prompt: A fictional research meeting discusses a proposal to screen all first-episode referrals with a self-disorder interview, on the grounds that the construct aggregates in the schizophrenia spectrum and predicted transition in an ultra-high-risk cohort. A statistician asks what would be needed before it could guide a service. Which answer is best supported by the cited literature?
questions.answer: A threshold validated in a comparable population with the outcome base rate and the proportions of people above and below it who later receive the diagnosis, plus evidence that the assessment adds information beyond a standard clinical interview.
questions.distractor: Nothing further, because the construct has demonstrated internal consistency, a single factor and a statistically significant predictive model, which together establish that the instrument measures the vulnerability directly.
questions.correction: Those three results are properties of the instrument and of particular samples, not of the individual case. The 100-admission study established aggregation across diagnostic groups with one factor and good internal consistency; the ultra-high-risk study followed only 49 participants for about 569 days and reported a Cox model rather than threshold performance; and the field's own critical paper lists specificity and structure as unresolved, noting that closely related disturbances appear in borderline personality disorder and that comparisons across psychoses had not been made. Prediction in a cohort is not prediction for the next person, and the missing quantities are exactly the positive and negative predictive values at a stated cut-off.

questions.prompt: A fictional service compares mean depression scores across two language versions of the same scale and announces that speakers of language B are more distressed, because their mean is two points higher. A colleague asks what would make that inference safe. What does lesson 73 require?
questions.answer: Evidence that the scale is measurement-invariant across the two language versions — that items function equivalently at equal underlying severity — before the mean difference is interpreted as a difference in distress; a cross-group mean comparison is uninterpretable until item functioning has been tested.
questions.distractor: A test-retest reliability coefficient above 0.8 in each language version, since a reliable scale gives a trustworthy comparison.
questions.correction: Reliability in each group separately does not license comparison between groups: both could be internally consistent while an item reads differently in one language, so that equal severity produces unequal scores. The four-country study of the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 is the model here, because it checked dimensionality, reliability and differential item functioning before reporting higher latent means in some countries; the finding of largely equivalent item functioning is what made the mean difference interpretable. Two additional cautions from the same lesson: the comparison also depends on the samples being equivalent in other ways, and a two-point mean difference should be read against the instrument's measurement error and its instrument-specific minimal important difference.

questions.prompt: A fictional committee is asked to decide whether to adopt a proposed refinement of an existing diagnosis. The evidence presented is that the refined criteria identify a more homogeneous group in the authors' sample, and that kappa agreement between raters using the refinement was 0.71. Which is the missing element a revising body would expect?
questions.answer: A comparison with the incumbent criteria under validators agreed in advance — for example course of illness, family aggregation or treatment response — showing that the refinement performs better, since agreement and internal homogeneity are not evidence that the category picks out something more coherent.
questions.distractor: A larger reliability study, because kappa of 0.71 falls below the threshold traditionally treated as good agreement and must first be raised above 0.8.
questions.correction: The committee should indeed look at the reliability evidence, but the study of reliability methods shows how much such a figure depends on design: in one programme, mean kappa was 0.80 using audio-recording review and 0.47 using test-retest, with about a quarter of test-retest estimates poor, and the DSM-5 dispute turned on which benchmark to apply rather than on arithmetic. So 0.71 is not self-evidently a problem, and raising it is not the missing piece. What a revising body owes the field, on Kendler's standard, is evidence that the new criteria improve on the predecessor using an agreed set of validators, which is also the ambition of the original validation programme. Homogeneity within a sample of people selected to be homogeneous is close to a restatement of the criteria.

questions.prompt: A fictional clinician reads two summaries of the same intervention: a 2011 review reporting a moderate pooled effect, and a 2019 update of the same literature reporting a smaller effect, noting that the earlier pooled estimate included several trials that had not been prospectively registered. What is the most defensible interpretation, and what would she look for next?
questions.answer: The shrinkage is the expected consequence of a literature in which some trials were not verifiably pre-specified, so the earlier estimate was probably inflated; she should check whether the update accounted for missing or selectively reported results and whether the underlying trials were registered prospectively.
questions.distractor: The intervention's effect has probably declined over time in the population, since pooled effects from later reviews are generally lower than earlier ones for biological or social reasons.
questions.correction: A secular decline in effectiveness is a possible explanation but it is not the first one to test, and it requires its own evidence such as a trend analysis relating effect size to calendar period with trial-level covariates. The structural explanation is better supported: prospective registration is what makes pre-specification checkable, and in the psychiatric journals that required it, only 60 of 181 trials (33.1%) met the standard in a window covering 2009 to 2013, with 11.6% unregistered and 33.7% registered retrospectively. Selective and incomplete reporting truncates the distribution of results toward the positive, which inflates a pooled average, exactly the mechanism analysed at the level of probability by Ioannidis and measured for antidepressant trials in the following lesson. The next things to check are the appraisals the update used: risk of bias, publication-bias assessment and certainty grading (lesson 77).

units.title: Reading treatment evidence and reasoning about services

lessons.title: Average effects and the person in front of you: heterogeneity, subgroups and individual prediction
lessons.explanation:
A randomised trial answers one question well: did this intervention, on average, change this outcome in this population under these conditions? It does not answer the question a clinician is actually asked, which is what will happen to this person. Education only; nothing here recommends treatment for anyone.

Begin with the definition of the problem. In a widely cited framework for reporting heterogeneity of treatment effect, Kent and colleagues observe that the balance between treatment risks and benefits may differ substantially between large identifiable patient subgroups, and that the average benefit observed in the summary result may even be non-representative of the treatment effect for a typical patient in the trial [1]. That sentence is stronger than the usual 'responders vary'. Non-representative means that if you describe the trial's effect to the average participant in the trial, you can be wrong — because in the presence of variation, the average effect need not describe anyone in particular.

Two kinds of subgroup analysis follow from that, and the framework distinguishes them by what they model. A risk-modelling approach uses a multivariable model to predict the risk of the outcome and then disaggregates trial participants by predicted risk, on the idea that absolute benefit typically varies more with baseline risk than with anything else. An effect-modelling approach adds an interaction term and lets the data estimate how treatment effect itself varies with patient characteristics [1]. The Predictive Approaches to Treatment effect Heterogeneity statement formalises these as the two families, recommending risk-based heterogeneity analysis as the priority and asking that other subgroup analyses be labelled explicitly for what they are — primary, if well motivated by prior evidence and intended to inform decisions, or exploratory otherwise [2].

Why be strict? Because conventional subgroup analyses are weak. Kent and colleagues state plainly that such analyses are usually unable to detect even large variations in treatment effect, since the interaction test has far less power than the main effect it is embedded in [1]. Burke and colleagues quantify the epistemic problem: even when subgroup-effect power is excellent, at 80%, reaching an 80% true positive threshold requires a prior probability of about 20% [3]. In plain terms, a subgroup claim discovered by searching a big trial is probably noise unless someone had a strong reason to expect it beforehand. This is not an argument against subgroups; it is an argument that the reason to believe a subgroup result has to come from outside the trial, in advance.

Then the arithmetic that makes all of this clinically visible. Relative effects are fairly stable across risk groups; absolute effects are not. Illustrative calculation, not a property of any named treatment: suppose an intervention reduces the risk of an event by 25% in relative terms. At a baseline risk of 40%, the treated risk is 30.0% and the absolute reduction is 10.0 percentage points, which is a number needed to treat of about 10.0. At a baseline risk of 8%, the treated risk is 6.0% and the absolute reduction is 2.0 points, an NNT of about 50.0. At 2%, the absolute reduction is 0.5 points and the NNT is about 200.0. Same relative effect, same trial, same paper — and a twenty-fold difference in how much work is needed to prevent one event. This is why risk-based analysis is prioritised: it does not require effect modification to be useful, only variation in baseline risk, which is nearly always present.

Finally, separate three things that get collapsed in advertising. Prognostic markers predict outcome regardless of treatment: they tell you who will do badly, which is useful for care planning and useless for choosing between treatments. Predictive markers, properly defined, identify differential benefit — and these are rare and mostly unproven in psychiatry. Individual prediction is a fourth thing again, and it needs more than a subgroup effect: it needs a model validated in the target population, with calibrated absolute risks and a demonstration that acting on it improves outcomes. What the evidence base mostly offers is the first, described as though it were the third.
lessons.example:
Worked reasoning on a fictional clinical dilemma, showing where the average effect stops helping and what a defensible decision looks like.

A 62-year-old man with a long history of recurrent depression has had two episodes that responded partially to a psychological therapy delivered in a trial setting, and now relapses whenever he stops attending. His clinician has three options on the desk: continue the therapy he has already had, switch to a different therapy with a smaller evidence base, or add a supervised structured activity programme from a trial that reported an average benefit.

Step one: classify the evidence by what it estimates. The repeated therapy's evidence base is an average effect in a population that included people like him, which licenses the statement that the treatment works on average and not the statement that it will work again for him; past partial response is a prognostic observation, which the framework in lesson 76 would classify as risk-relevant rather than predictive [1]. The alternative therapy's evidence base is smaller and possibly single-trial, so its average is estimated with more uncertainty, and the relevant question is not 'which is bigger' but 'is the difference between them estimable at all'.

Step two: ask whether any of the options' evidence includes a pre-specified moderation analysis. If the activity programme's trial reported that benefit was confined to people above a severity threshold, and that analysis was exploratory, the honest reading is a hypothesis: the subgroup could be real, and it could be a finding of the kind that needs a prior probability near 20% to be credible even with good power [3]. That does not make it useless — hypotheses are how knowledge starts — but it changes the words used with the patient from 'this works for people like you' to 'this looked more promising in people with more severe symptoms, and we do not know whether that holds'.

Step three: apply the absolute arithmetic. Suppose the programme's reported relative reduction is 30% for a relapse outcome. If his baseline risk over a year is 50%, the absolute reduction is 15 points and the NNT is about 7, computed with the same ratio as the illustration above; if his baseline risk is 10%, the absolute reduction is 3 points and the NNT is about 33. Deciding that the programme is 'worth 30%' is a different decision in each case, and the trial's average risk determines which of those two the trial actually tested.

Step four: state what would change the decision, and write it down. For a clinician working with a person rather than with a mean, the defensible formulation is: try the option with the best-supported average, define in advance how long a fair trial of it is, define what improvement would look like for this person, specify what would trigger a switch, and record the uncertainty in those terms. Nothing in this lesson says any of the three options is right; it says which parts of the evidence can bear such a statement and which cannot.
lessons.question: A fictional paper reports: 'In our randomised trial, the intervention reduced relapse overall. In a subgroup analysis, men over 55 appeared to benefit more than others (interaction p = 0.04). We recommend targeting the intervention at men over 55.' Which criticism is best supported by the sources in this lesson?
lessons.answer: An exploratory interaction test from a single trial is a hypothesis rather than a recommendation; the credibility of a subgroup claim depends on prior evidence and adequate power, and risk-based analysis of absolute benefit is usually more informative than an effect-modification claim of this kind.
lessons.distractor: The recommendation is invalid because subgroup analyses should never be reported, since any division of a randomised sample destroys randomisation and makes the analysis no better than observational.
lessons.correction: The distractor overstates the case and misstates the reason. Randomisation protects the overall comparison; a subgroup analysis of a randomised trial remains randomised within the subgroup, which is why such analyses are conducted — the problems are multiplicity, low power for interactions, and post hoc motivation. Kent and colleagues' framework treats subgroup analyses as useful when they are explicitly labelled: primary analyses, well motivated by prior evidence and intended to inform decisions, versus the rest [2], and notes that conventional subgroup analyses are usually unable to detect even large variations in treatment effect [1]. Burke and colleagues' prior-probability result makes the arithmetic concrete: a subgroup finding needs a strong pre-existing reason to be believed [3]. The final clause of the distractor's claim is also wrong in a different way: observational comparisons are not equivalent to randomised subgroup analyses, because the former confound the characteristic with everything associated with it.

depth.definitions:
Average treatment effect: the mean difference in outcome between arms in a trial population, which is what randomisation licenses. Heterogeneity of treatment effect (HTE): variation in treatment effect across patients. Risk-based heterogeneity: variation in absolute benefit arising from variation in baseline risk; effect-based heterogeneity: variation in the treatment effect itself, estimated with interaction terms [1][2]. Relative versus absolute effect: a proportionate reduction versus the difference in event rates, from which NNT is derived. Prognostic versus predictive marker: a characteristic associated with outcome regardless of treatment versus one associated with differential treatment benefit. Pre-specification: whether an analysis was committed to before data collection, which is the line between a primary and an exploratory subgroup analysis [2]. Precision or personalised medicine in psychiatry: a family of claims that individual-level prediction, usually from models or biomarkers, should guide treatment selection; the standard such claims must meet is stated in the lesson's final paragraph.

Prerequisite: lesson 73 on measurement and interpretability, which supplies the vocabulary for what a change score means; lesson 75 on the published record, which explains why single-trial subgroup findings deserve the scepticism applied here.
depth.mechanism:
Why does the average stop describing the individual, and what can be done about it? Three mechanisms and one hard limit.

Mechanism one: baseline risk varies, and absolute benefit scales with it. Because the relative effect of most interventions is comparatively stable across risk strata while the absolute difference is not, disaggregating a trial by predicted risk usually reveals substantial variation in absolute benefit without requiring any interaction to exist [1][2]. This is the cheapest and most robust route to useful heterogeneity, and it explains why risk-based analysis is prioritised over hunting for subgroups.

Mechanism two: interactions exist but are hard to detect. An interaction test estimates a difference between differences, and its standard error inherits the standard errors of both subgroup estimates; the power to detect an interaction is therefore far lower than the power to detect the main effect, which is why Kent and colleagues say conventional subgroup analyses are usually unable to detect even large variations [1]. The practical consequence is asymmetric: a null interaction is weak evidence of no heterogeneity, and a significant interaction found by searching is weak evidence of heterogeneity.

Mechanism three: annotation and multiplicity. A trial with several outcomes and several candidate moderators generates many tests; some will cross a threshold by chance. Pre-specification and labelled primacy convert this from a nuisance into a structure for interpretation [2], which is why the PATH statement's recommendation is about labelling and priority rather than about banning analyses.

The hard limit: even a well-validated predictive model does not tell you what to do. Selecting treatment by predicted benefit changes outcomes only if the model is calibrated in the target population, if the treatments genuinely differ in their effects for the predicted groups, and if acting on the prediction is better than the alternative strategies — including treating everyone or using a stepped approach. Claims of individualised treatment selection in psychiatry almost always fall short at the third step, which is a statement about the current evidence base rather than a claim that individual prediction is impossible.
depth.secondExample:
A contrasting application where heterogeneity is real, well established and expressed as a baseline-risk effect rather than as an interaction — which is why it is easy to miss.

Consider a fictional service evaluating a structured relapse-prevention programme for people leaving hospital after an admission for a psychotic disorder. The trial's overall result is a modest reduction in readmission over eighteen months, with a confidence interval that includes no effect. Read naively, the trial is 'negative' and the programme is not adopted.

Now disaggregate by predicted baseline risk using a multivariable model fitted to the control arm. Two groups emerge: people with a high predicted risk of readmission (say, predicted probability around 50% over eighteen months) and people with a low predicted risk (around 10%). Ill-illustrative arithmetic, using the same 25% relative reduction as earlier: for the high-risk group, a 50% baseline becomes about 37.5% with the programme, an absolute reduction of about 12.5 points and an NNT of about 8; for the low-risk group, 10% becomes about 7.5%, an absolute reduction of 2.5 points and an NNT of about 40. The overall average benefit mixes these two very different numbers in proportions determined by the trial's case mix. Note carefully what has and has not been claimed: no interaction has been estimated, no subgroup was hunted, and the variation comes from baseline risk, which is measurable in a service and is the kind of heterogeneity the framework tells you to expect [1][2].

Where this reasoning can still go wrong is stated plainly in the literature: the risk model must have been developed and validated for the relevant population, and the disaggregation is a re-analysis of the same data, so it should generate a hypothesis to be tested prospectively rather than a final allocation rule. A service that adopts it should record exactly who it is being adopted for, what predicted risk threshold justifies it, and what will be measured to check whether the prediction held [2]. The transferable contrast with the previous example: risk-based heterogeneity is usually estimable from existing trials and is often the honest answer to 'who benefits most'; effect-based subgroup claims require a prior reason to be credible [1][3].
depth.mistake:
Misconception one: that an average effect applies to each individual to the same degree. Kent and colleagues' formulation is the correction — the average may not even describe a typical participant when effects vary [1] — and the remedy is to work with absolute benefit at the person's baseline risk rather than with the headline percentage.

Misconception two: that a statistically significant interaction identifies the people who benefit. It identifies a group in which the difference between arms was larger, in a particular sample, with a test that has low power and no protection against multiplicity; the PATH statement's answer is to label such analyses by their provenance and priority rather than to accept them as decision rules [2]. Burke and colleagues' prior-probability requirement is the sharpest available statement of the same point [3].

Misconception three, in the opposite direction: that because individual prediction is oversold, treatment decisions should ignore prognostic information altogether. They should not: baseline risk determines absolute benefit and is usually the most actionable piece of information available, and prognosis shapes care planning and the intensity of follow-up whether or not it modifies treatment effect. Diagnostic correction: when you see the word 'personalised' in a psychiatric abstract, determine whether the analysis was prognostic, risk-based, effect-based or a genuine out-of-sample individual prediction model, and require absolute risks with confidence intervals before accepting a selection claim.
depth.application:
Nonblocking task. A fictional trial reports: overall relative risk reduction for relapse 20% (95% CI 5% to 33%); exploratory subgroup analysis suggests a larger effect in participants with childhood adversity (interaction p = 0.03); a risk model from the same data identifies a high-risk third of participants with predicted relapse risk 45% versus 12% in the rest. Write a 200-word summary for a service that must decide whether to offer the intervention to everyone, to the high-risk third only, or to wait. Include: the absolute effects at both risk levels (use the 20% relative reduction); what the subgroup result may and may not support; and the single condition that would most change your advice.

Model response. Absolute effects, computed from the stated 20% relative reduction: in the high-risk group, 45% falls to 36%, an absolute reduction of 9 percentage points, an NNT of about 11; in the lower-risk group, 12% falls to 9.6%, an absolute reduction of 2.4 points, an NNT of about 42. So the same intervention is roughly four times more efficient in the high-risk group — evidence for targeting that rests on baseline risk rather than on an interaction, which is the kind of analysis the framework prioritises [1][2]. The subgroup result may support a hypothesis worth testing prospectively and does not support a decision rule: it was exploratory, the interaction has low power, and a single interaction test at p = 0.03 in one trial would need a strong prior reason to be believed [3]. The condition that would most change the advice: external validation of the risk model in this service's own population — if the predicted risks do not hold, the absolute benefits, and therefore the efficiency argument for targeting, dissolve. A secondary condition worth naming: evidence on harms and burden by risk group, since a decision based only on benefit can mislead.

Rubric: 1 point for computing both absolute risks correctly and stating NNTs; 1 for attributing the targeting argument to baseline risk rather than to the subgroup finding; 1 for requiring external validation before adopting the threshold; 1 for naming at least one thing the decision needs besides benefit. Three or four points means the average-effect-to-individual gap is being reasoned rather than recited.
depth.summary:
Trials estimate average effects; average effects can fail to describe anyone in particular when effects vary [1]. The two defensible routes to heterogeneity are risk-based analysis, which does not require effect modification, and explicitly labelled effect-based analyses, which do [1][2]; conventional subgroup hunting is weak because interactions are underpowered [1] and because credibility depends on prior probability [3]. Absolute benefit depends on baseline risk, so the same relative reduction produces NNTs that differ by an order of magnitude across risk strata.

Transfer: this lesson is the bridge between the measurement questions of unit 1 and the evidence-appraisal questions of the rest of unit 2. The next lesson asks how the published record itself was assembled and whether the average it reports can be trusted, which is the prior question to every heterogeneity analysis above.
