Then read the proposed framework distinguishing risk-based from effect-based heterogeneity and the reporting recommendations.

readings.title: Kent, D. M. et al. (2020), 'The Predictive Approaches to Treatment effect Heterogeneity (PATH) Statement', Annals of Internal Medicine 172(1):35-45 — PMC7531587
readings.note: Read the abstract and the recommendations: the risk-modelling and effect-modelling approaches, the priority given to multivariable risk-based analysis, and the requirement that other subgroup analyses be explicitly labelled as primary or exploratory. Use this to check the lesson's claim about labelling rather than banning subgroup analyses.

readings.title: Burke, J. F., Sussman, J. B., Kent, D. M. & Hayward, R. A. (2015), 'Three simple rules to ensure reasonably credible subgroup analyses', BMJ 351:h5651 — PMC4632208
readings.note: Read the paper's treatment of power and prior probability, including the statement used in this lesson that even with excellent subgroup-effect power of 80%, reaching an 80% true positive threshold requires a prior probability of about 20%; and the recommendation to conduct multivariable risk-based analyses of trials with positive overall results and of negative trials where the intervention has plausible harm. Note: the lesson cites this source for the prior-probability point and does not reproduce the paper's numbered rules, which should be read in the original.

visual.title: Six labelled steps from a trial's average result to a defensible statement about one person
visual.description: A reasoning sequence for translating an average treatment effect into an absolute effect for a specific baseline risk, with the point at which each step can go wrong.
steps: Step 1 — Locate the estimate: identify the population, the comparator, the outcome and the time horizon of the reported average effect. Failure point: describing a trial's average as though it applied to any patient meeting the entry criteria.

Step 2 — Convert to absolute terms: apply the relative effect to the person's baseline risk to get an absolute reduction and an NNT. Failure point: quoting a relative reduction as a benefit without the baseline risk, which hides a twenty-fold range in efficiency.

Step 3 — Separate prognosis from prediction: ask whether the characteristic you are using predicts outcome regardless of treatment or modifies treatment effect. Failure point: using a prognostic marker as though it identified who benefits.

Step 4 — Check the provenance of any heterogeneity claim: was the analysis risk-based or effect-based, pre-specified as primary, or exploratory? Failure point: treating a searched interaction as a decision rule; an interaction needs a prior reason to be credible.

Step 5 — Look for the fourth requirement before claiming individual prediction: calibration in the target population, absolute risks with intervals, and evidence that acting on the prediction beats not acting on it. Failure point: accepting a model's discrimination statistic as evidence that selecting treatment by it improves outcomes.

Step 6 — Write the decision with its revisability: state the option chosen, the trial period, what improvement means for this person, and what would justify switching. Failure point: presenting a decision as though the evidence determined it.

lessons.title: The published record as a biased sample: reporting bias, meta-analysis and certainty
lessons.explanation:
Lesson 75 showed that a trial's result can be distorted before it is written. This lesson is about what happens afterwards: how results are selected into the literature, how a meta-analysis can inherit that selection, and what appraisal tools are supposed to do about it. Education only; nothing here is treatment advice.

The strongest available evidence on reporting bias in psychiatry comes from comparing what was published with what was submitted to a regulator. Turner and colleagues used trial reports in US Food and Drug Administration drug approval packages as a gold standard, identified 30 phase II/III double-blind placebo-controlled acute monotherapy trials involving 13,747 patients across four newer antidepressants, then located the corresponding published reports [1]. Among the newer antidepressants, transparent publication — where the conclusion in the published paper agreed with the FDA's — occurred for 15 of 15 positive trials (100%) but only 7 of 15 negative trials (47%), an improvement on the earlier cohort but still asymmetric [1]. The consequence for a reader is visible in their meta-analytic comparison: the FDA-based effect size was 0.24 (95% CI 0.18 to 0.30) while the journal-based effect size was 0.29 (95% CI 0.23 to 0.36), so effect size inflation attributable to reporting bias was 0.05 for the newer cohort and 0.10 for the older one [1]. The authors also report that transparent reporting increased from 11% to 47% across cohorts [1]. Two lessons sit in that single study: reporting bias materially inflates apparent efficacy, and the direction of travel has improved without reaching symmetry.

The same phenomenon has been measured directly for psychological treatments. Driessen and colleagues examined US National Institute of Mental Health-funded trials of psychological treatment for major depressive disorder, comparing published and unpublished trials; among comparisons to control conditions, adding unpublished studies (Hedges' g = 0.20; 95% CI -0.11 to 0.51; k = 6) to the published studies (g = 0.52; 0.37 to 0.68; k = 20) reduced the pooled effect size point estimate to 0.39 (0.08 to 0.70), a reduction of 25%, and the authors note their findings may overestimate the effect for further reasons [2]. Notice the shape of that result: the unpublished studies were not merely nonsignificant, their pooled estimate was near zero. A meta-analysis of the published literature would have reported 0.52 and been wrong by more than a quarter, not through any analytic mistake but because of which studies existed to be analysed.

So how is bias detected? Funnel plots and their tests are the standard visual and statistical approach, and the authoritative guidance is more cautious than the practice it describes. Sterne and colleagues state that funnel plot asymmetry should not be equated with publication bias, because it has a number of other possible causes, and they recommend that these tests should not be used when there are fewer than 10 studies in the meta-analysis, because test power is usually too low to distinguish chance from real asymmetry; in some situations, such as substantial heterogeneity, the minimum number may be substantially more than 10 [3]. That is an unusually exact set of constraints to carry around, and it matters because the small meta-analyses common in psychiatric topics cannot support a formal claim either way.

Two further tools belong in the same paragraph. Risk-of-bias assessment is a structured, domain-based appraisal of individual trials; the current version of the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomised trials, RoB 2, is published with variants for cluster and crossover designs on the tool's own site, which is the place to read the current domain list rather than relying on recollection [4]. And certainty grading, through GRADE, assesses confidence in an estimate for each important outcome and expresses it in four categories — high, moderate, low and very low — with explicit, comprehensive criteria for rating up and down, including risk of bias, inconsistency of results, indirectness of evidence, imprecision, and publication bias [5]. The handbook is emphatic that this is not a formula: the factors are not discrete categories but continua within and among categories, and where a body of evidence sits near a threshold, whether to rate down depends on judgement [5].

Assemble the three findings and you have the reader's version of the problem. Meta-analysis is arithmetic on a sample of studies, and if that sample was selected on the basis of its results, the arithmetic produces a precise number with a misleading centre; the tools designed to detect this are weakest precisely where psychiatric evidence bases are thinnest; and certainty grading exists to translate the resulting uncertainty into language a decision-maker can use, at the cost of asking appraisers to make judgements the grade alone does not determine.
lessons.example:
Worked reasoning on two fictional meta-analyses of the same question, to show how appraisal changes the conclusion without changing the numbers.

Question: does a certain psychosocial intervention reduce hospital readmission? Meta-analysis X pools twelve published trials, reports a pooled risk ratio of 0.78 (95% CI 0.66 to 0.92), creates a funnel plot, notes mild asymmetry, and concludes that the intervention is effective. Meta-analysis Y pools nineteen trials — the same twelve plus seven identified from a trial registry, four of them unpublished — and reports a pooled risk ratio of 0.93 (95% CI 0.79 to 1.09), concluding that the evidence is uncertain.

Step one: check whether the difference is an analytic dispute or a sampling dispute. The two analyses used overlapping methods; the substantive difference is which studies were included. That is the pattern the Turner comparison makes visible with regulators' files [1] and the Driessen comparison makes visible with funders' files [2], where adding unpublished trials moved a pooled estimate from 0.52 to 0.39 on a standardized scale. When two syntheses of one question disagree, the first question to ask is what the second one found that the first did not.

Step two: check whether the asymmetry claim could carry weight. Meta-analysis X has twelve studies, so a formal asymmetry test is permissible under the guidance, but only just, and the guidance warns that asymmetry has multiple causes beyond publication bias — heterogeneity in populations, differences in risk of bias, and even chance [3]. In this case a plausible non-publication cause is visible: the registered trials in Y were larger and multi-site, while several of X's trials were small single-site studies of the kind that produce more extreme estimates. Small-study effects can arise from genuine differences in what small studies examine, not only from selective publication, which is exactly why the guidance refuses the equation between asymmetry and bias [3].

Step three: grade the certainty rather than announcing a verdict. Following the handbook's structure, the appraisal for Y would start from randomised trials (nominally high), then consider rating down: risk of bias (several trials unblinded outcome assessors, which the RoB 2 domains would handle by reporting a per-trial judgement [4]), inconsistency (if effects vary widely across trials), indirectness (if the intervention in several trials was not the one the service would deliver), imprecision (the confidence interval crosses the decision threshold), and publication bias (present, as shown by the discrepancy between X and Y) [5]. Any single one of these might justify rating down one level; the aggregate often justifies more. The handbook's insistence that these are continua and judgement calls rather than ticks [5] is what makes the process defensible and also what makes it contestable — a body of evidence can be graded moderate by one panel and low by another, and both can be behaving properly.

Step four: say what a decision-maker should do with this. Not 'the intervention works' and not 'the evidence is worthless', but: the best estimate is closer to no effect than the published-only estimate suggested; the confidence interval is compatible with a modest benefit and with harm; the certainty is low to moderate at best; and the choice therefore depends on cost, burden and what else is available — considerations GRADE explicitly separates from the evidence itself [5]. Notice how much of the reasoning was about studies that were never read, which is the central difficulty of this lesson.
lessons.question: A fictional reviewer writes: 'Our funnel plot is asymmetric, so publication bias is proven, and a GRADE rating of low confirms the treatment does not work.' Which correction addresses both errors at once?
lessons.answer: Asymmetry is consistent with publication bias but has other causes and cannot be treated as proof, especially with few studies; and a low certainty rating expresses limited confidence in the estimate rather than evidence that the treatment is ineffective — the estimate may be compatible with benefit, harm or nothing.
lessons.distractor: Both statements are correct in substance: asymmetry is the standard test for publication bias, and a low GRADE rating is conventionally read as evidence of absence of effect.
lessons.correction: The guidance is explicit on the first point: funnel plot asymmetry should not be equated with publication bias because it has a number of other possible causes, and these tests should not be used with fewer than 10 studies, with the minimum often substantially higher when heterogeneity is substantial [3]. On the second point, GRADE rates confidence in the estimated effect for each important outcome on four levels and provides explicit criteria for rating down, including imprecision — an estimate whose confidence interval crosses the threshold of clinical relevance [5]. Low certainty therefore says the estimate could easily be different, which cuts both ways: an estimate consistent with a worthwhile benefit would be rated down for imprecision but still supports the benefit. The confusion of 'we are unsure' with 'there is nothing there' is one of the most consequential errors in reading psychiatric evidence, because it removes exactly the information a decision needs, which is the range of plausible effects.

depth.definitions:
Reporting bias: distortion of the literature arising from which results are published, how they are reported, and which outcomes are selected. Publication bias: the specific case where the probability of publication depends on the direction or significance of the result [3]. Outcome reporting bias: selective reporting of outcomes or analyses within published studies, the phenomenon prospective registration exists to detect (lesson 75). Gold-standard comparison: comparing the published record against a complete record of trials held by a funder or regulator, as in the FDA approval packages used by Turner and colleagues [1] and the funder files used by Driessen and colleagues [2]. Funnel plot: a scatter plot of study effect size against precision, whose asymmetry may indicate small-study effects of various origins. Small-study effects: the tendency for smaller studies to show larger effects, which can arise from publication bias, heterogeneity, or differential quality. Risk of bias: a structured judgement about whether a trial's estimate is likely biased, made domain by domain with RoB 2 or an equivalent tool [4]. Certainty of evidence: GRADE's judgement, per outcome, that the estimate is high, moderate, low or very low confidence, with defined reasons for rating down (risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias) and up [5].

Prerequisite: lesson 75 for pre-specification, plagiarism-free replication, and the registration figures; lesson 73 for measurement error and interpretability, which is what 'imprecision' partly quantifies.
depth.mechanism:
Why does the published record distort, and why is the distortion so hard to see from inside the literature?

The selection happens in a specific order. A trial is conducted and produces a result. Whether it enters the record depends on the result's direction and size, on the sponsor's interests and filing obligations, on authors' competing demands, and on editors' preferences. Turner's comparison measures one step of this most cleanly, because the FDA holds the complete set of trials that sponsors must submit: among newly approved antidepressants, adherence between published conclusions and regulatory conclusions was 100% for positive trials and 47% for negative ones, and the pooled estimate from the published record exceeded the FDA-based estimate by 0.05, down from 0.10 in the earlier cohort [1]. The improvement is real and the residual asymmetry is also real.

The second mechanism, outcome reporting bias, does not require a study to be missing: the study is published, and the reported analysis is not the one that was pre-specified. This is why registration matters and why the registration compliance figures of lesson 75 bound what any reader could have detected [4]. It also explains why a meta-analysis pooling published results can be internally sound and externally wrong: pooling is arithmetic over the studies that exist.

Detection is limited by statistics, not by diligence. The funnel-plot tests assume a relationship between study size and precision, and with few studies their power is too low to separate chance from real asymmetry; the guidance therefore sets a floor of about ten studies and warns that the floor rises with heterogeneity [3]. The consequence should be stated plainly: for most psychiatric questions, the honest position is 'bias is plausible and unquantified', not 'bias was excluded'.

GRADE's mechanism is different. It does not detect bias; it converts the appraiser's judgements about a body of evidence into a shared vocabulary, then separates that judgement from the recommendation, which depends additionally on values, costs, feasibility and equity [5]. Its decision to express the result in four levels rather than a continuous score is a deliberate refusal of false precision; the handbook's own statement that the factors are continua and that rating decisions depend on judgement [5] is what makes panels disagree, and is also what keeps the disagreements visible.
depth.secondExample:
A contrasting case in which the bias runs the other way — towards understating an effect — which is important because the lesson's material can otherwise be read as a one-directional scepticism.

Consider a fictional evaluation of a service change rather than a drug: a crisis team that keeps people out of hospital. The evidence available is a set of before-and-after audits from services that introduced the model and reported their own results. Almost by construction, the audits that survive to publication are from services where the model was implemented well: trusts that failed to staff it either do not write it up or write it up internally. The published record therefore over-represents well-implemented services, which inflates the apparent effect — the same direction as the drug example — but now the *mechanism* is implementation selection rather than result-based publication.

Now take the opposite case: a trial whose primary outcome is a structured diagnostic interview administered by assessors who know the treatment allocation, and whose authors report a null result for the primary outcome and a positive result on a self-report measure. Suppose the null is genuine and the positive is noise. The literature will over-report benefit here too. But suppose instead that the trial's null result reflects a measurement that is insensitive to change, while the treatment genuinely helps. Now the published record understates the benefit, and no amount of funnel-plot reasoning will reveal it, because the problem is inside every study rather than in which studies exist.

Both directions are real, and the appraisal machinery is asymmetric in what it can detect. Selection-based bias leaves traces (incompleteness relative to registries and regulators [1][4]; asymmetry in funnel plots [3]). Within-study problems such as insensitive measures, mis-specified outcomes or unblinded assessment leave no such trace and are addressed by the domain-level risk-of-bias judgements [4] and by the rating-down criteria for indirectness and imprecision [5] — which is to say, by judgement rather than by test. The transferable comparison: when you find yourself concluding 'the published evidence overstates the effect', you have a mechanism to name; when you conclude the opposite, name the mechanism too, or you are simply asserting.
depth.mistake:
Misconception one: that meta-analysis corrects bias. It does not; it summarises a sample, and if the sample is selected, the summary is biased and confident. The Driessen comparison is the clearest demonstration available in psychological treatment research: adding six unpublished comparisons to twenty published ones moved the pooled estimate from 0.52 to 0.39, a reduction of about a quarter [2]. A systematic review is a method for assembling evidence with known rules, and its value depends on how completely it did so.

Misconception two: that a funnel plot settles it. The guidance says asymmetry should not be equated with publication bias because it has other possible causes, and sets the ten-study floor for testing [3]; a study whose asymmetry stems from heterogeneity in populations or from small trials being conducted differently has not thereby shown selective publication.

Misconception three: that a GRADE rating is a measurement of quality, so that low certainty means bad studies. It is confidence in an estimate for a stated outcome, expressed on four levels, with five named reasons for rating down and the explicit statement that the factors are continua requiring judgement [5]. Two appraisers working honestly can land on different levels, and the right response to that is to ask which downgrading factor they weighed differently — not to treat the grade as an objective output.

Practical diagnostic correction: when a paper's abstract says an effect is 'supported by meta-analysis', look for three things before believing anything — whether the search included unpublished and registered trials [1][2], whether the number of studies permits any asymmetry assessment [3], and whether a certainty rating was made per outcome [5]. If two of the three are absent, the abstract is reporting arithmetic, not evidence.
depth.application:
Nonblocking task. You are given three fictional resources for one clinical question: (a) a published meta-analysis of nine trials, pooled standardized effect 0.55, no certainty rating, funnel plot described as 'broadly symmetric'; (b) a drug regulator's trial-by-trial summary showing the same nine published trials plus four further trials with near-zero effects; (c) a guideline that rates the evidence for the outcome as moderate and notes imprecision. Write a 180-word appraisal that: states your best estimate of the effect and why it differs from (a); assesses whether (a) could have detected the discrepancy using its own methods; and rates the confidence you would attach to a claim of clinically worthwhile benefit.

Model response. Best estimate: materially below 0.55, and closer to the regulator-based pooled figure, because (b) is a complete record of trials for the same question rather than a sample of them, and the published-only estimate is inflated by an unknown but plausibly substantial amount — the same pattern and mechanism documented for antidepressants (FDA-based 0.24 versus journal-based 0.29) and for psychological treatment of depression (0.52 including only published trials versus 0.39 with unpublished trials added) [1][2]. Could (a) have detected it? No, or not reliably: with nine studies, a formal test for funnel plot asymmetry should not be used at all under the published guidance, since power is too low and the minimum number may be substantially higher when heterogeneity is present, and visual symmetry is not evidence of completeness [3]. Confidence in a worthwhile benefit: low to moderate at best, because the discrepancy itself is evidence of publication bias — one of GRADE's explicit reasons for rating down [5] — and imprecision compounds it; a defensible formulation is that a modest benefit remains compatible with the data, that the magnitude is uncertain, and that the decision should be made on that basis with the uncertainty recorded rather than resolved.

Rubric: 1 point for preferring the complete record and naming why; 1 for using the ten-study floor or the asymmetry caveat correctly rather than calling the funnel plot conclusive; 1 for connecting the discrepancy to a GRADE downgrade; 1 for a final statement that preserves the plausible range rather than declaring the treatment ineffective or proven. Three or four points indicates that appraisal and verdict are being kept apart.
depth.summary:
The literature is a selected sample. Regulator-anchored comparison shows the direction and size of the distortion on a real body of psychiatric evidence — 100% transparent reporting for positive trials versus 47% for negative ones, with pooled efficacy inflated by 0.05 in the newer cohort and 0.10 in the older [1] — and funder-anchored comparison shows the same effect for psychological treatment, where adding unpublished trials cut the pooled estimate by about a quarter [2]. Detection tools have documented limits: funnel-plot tests require roughly ten studies and asymmetry is not identical to bias [3]. Appraisal tools structure judgement rather than replacing it: risk of bias domain by domain [4], and certainty in four levels with five named reasons for rating down, applied by judgement to continua rather than to categories [5].

Transfer: the next lesson goes inside the studies that survived this filter and asks what the comparison condition in them actually does, which turns out to be one of the largest determinants of the effect sizes you have just been appraising.

visual.title: Six labelled stations showing how trials become a literature, and where appraisal intervenes
visual.description: A sequence from trial conduct to graded certainty, with the specific distortion at each station and the instrument that can detect it.
steps: Station 1 — A trial is run and a result exists. Distortion risk: outcome definitions and analysis choices (lesson 75). Detection: pre-registered protocol and analysis plan.

Station 2 — Results are submitted to a regulator or funder. Distortion risk: none at this stage in jurisdictions with mandatory submission; this is why regulator packages serve as a gold standard for what trials exist.

Station 3 — Results are written up for publication. Distortion risk: selective outcome reporting, spin in abstracts, and conclusions that disagree with the data — regulator comparison found agreement for 100% of positive trials but 47% of negative ones.

Station 4 — Results enter the journal literature; some trials never do. Distortion risk: publication bias, which inflates pooled estimates: 0.29 versus 0.24 on the regulator comparison, and 0.52 versus 0.39 for psychological treatment of depression.

Station 5 — The literature is synthesised. Distortion risk: a precise but biased pooled estimate; the funnel-plot check for small-study effects is underpowered below about ten studies and asymmetry has causes other than bias.

Station 6 — Appraisal and grading. Distortion risk: judgements presented as if they were measurements. Detection: per-outcome certainty ratings with named reasons for rating down (risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias), applied as continua.

lessons.title: What the control condition does: non-specific factors, expectancy and therapist effects
lessons.explanation:
Every effect size in the trial literature is a difference between conditions. This lesson examines the other side of that subtraction. It is education about how to read research, not advice about anyone's treatment, and it contains no prescribing or dosing information.

Start with the most striking measured asymmetry in the field. Kirsch and colleagues analysed data from trials submitted to the US Food and Drug Administration, including trials that were not published, and assessed linear and quadratic effects of initial severity on improvement in drug and placebo groups and on the drug-placebo difference. Their findings: the drug-placebo difference increased as a function of initial severity, rising from virtually no difference at moderate levels of depression to a relatively small difference at very severe levels, and the difference was relatively small even for severely depressed patients [1]. In the same analysis, the mean drug-placebo difference in improvement scores was 1.80 points on the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression, whereas the threshold they cite for clinically significant benefit is a difference of 3 points [1]. Two things must be said about that comparison. First, the clinical-significance threshold is a convention, not a law, and reasonable people argue about whether a 3-point difference is the right benchmark on a 17-item scale. Second, Kirsch's interpretation of the placebo response as capturing most of the measured benefit has been contested directly in the literature; the lesson's point is not that his reading is correct, but that the control arm is doing measurable, large work and that any effect size quoted without it is under-described.

The control condition also has names and they are not interchangeable. Furukawa and colleagues searched for randomised trials comparing cognitive behavioural therapies against various controls in the acute-phase treatment of depression and applied network meta-analysis, identifying 49 trials with 2,730 participants. They found the effect size estimates for the treatment substantively different depending on the control condition, and the odds ratio of response for no-treatment over waiting-list was 2.9 (95% CI 1.3 to 5.7) [2]. In other words, participants assigned to a waiting list did worse than participants assigned to nothing — the pattern the authors describe, in the paper's own title, as waiting list possibly acting as a nocebo condition. Now read their caveats, because they are a model of intellectual honesty: the quality of evidence, including publication bias, was less than ideal; none of the preplanned sensitivity analyses limited to high-quality studies could be conducted; and the significant differences did not persist in post hoc sensitivity analyses attempting to adjust for publication bias [2]. The conclusion they permit themselves is correspondingly modest — that there may be important differences in control conditions [2]. Take the shape of that argument seriously: a provocative, plausible finding, an honest statement of what could not be checked, and a hedged conclusion. That is what a provisional result looks like when written properly.

Then there is who delivers the treatment. A systematic review of therapist effects reports that across 27 different treatment groups, therapists accounted for an average of 8.6% of the outcome variance, and cites Wampold's earlier estimate of approximately 8% [4]. Any percentage of variance is easy to dismiss until it is compared with something: 8.6% of outcome variance attributable to the individual clinician is larger than most treatment-versus-control differences in psychotherapy research, and it means that a trial's headline effect is a property of its particular therapists as well as its particular protocol. The practical consequences run in both directions. A trial showing benefit says something about the therapy as delivered by trained, supervised, monitored clinicians; a service that reproduces the protocol without the supervision has changed the intervention, which is the fidelity problem that lesson 79 takes up at the level of services.

Finally, allegiance. Munder and colleagues conducted a meta-meta-analysis summarising all available meta-analytic estimates of the association between researcher allegiance and treatment outcome, including 30 meta-analyses and controlling for primary-study overlap. The mean allegiance-outcome association was r = .262 (p = .002, I² = 28.98%), which they characterise as a moderate effect size, and they report it as robust across moderators including treatment, population and type of allegiance assessment [3]. One further finding deserves its own sentence: allegiance towards the allegiance-bias hypothesis itself moderated the association [3]. Researchers who believed in the phenomenon found it more strongly — which is the cleanest available example of why the reader's question is always about the properties of a study rather than about the virtue of its authors.
lessons.example:
Worked reasoning on a fictional pair of trials of the same therapy, chosen to show how the control arm manufactures the headline.

Trial A: 120 adults with moderate depression, randomised to twelve sessions of a structured therapy or to a waiting list. Result: large between-group difference favouring therapy at eight weeks, reported as a substantial effect.

Trial B: 120 adults with moderate depression, randomised to twelve sessions of the same therapy or to a matched control condition consisting of the same number of appointments with the same clinicians, in which the content was general supportive conversation about daily activities. Result: a smaller between-group difference, with a confidence interval that includes no effect.

Step one: notice that the interventions were the same and the numbers were the same. The difference is entirely in what the therapy was compared with. Trial A's comparison includes everything the therapy provides — attention, structure, an appointment at a fixed time each week, contact with a person who takes an interest, a hopeful account of the problem — plus its specific techniques. Trial B's comparison keeps most of those and removes the techniques. Consistent with the network meta-analysis pattern, the choice of comparator changes effect size estimates substantively [2], and the waiting-list arm in the depression literature has been argued to act as a nocebo condition rather than as an inert baseline [2].

Step two: ask which comparison answers which question. If the question is 'should this person be offered something rather than nothing?', Trial A's comparison is relevant, in the way that any treatment decision is made against the alternative of no treatment. If the question is 'does this specific technique add value over a competent, engaged conversation?', only Trial B's comparison speaks to it. Effect sizes from A and B are not rival measurements of one quantity; they are measurements of two different quantities, and quoting them in the same sentence as though they were comparable is the commonest error in the secondary literature. This is the discipline the appraisal tools aim at: the certainty rating applies to a specific comparison, for a specific outcome, and the comparator is part of what is being rated (lesson 77).

Step three: think about where the non-specific effects come from, without collapsing into a story. Several sources are plausible and partly separable: expectancy and hope, the structured attention of a weekly appointment, regression to the mean in people recruited at their worst, spontaneous fluctuation in a condition that is episodic by nature, and measurement reactivity in scales completed by someone who knows they are being evaluated. Notice that the last of these is not 'the control arm doing something' but the measure responding to being measured, which is a lesson 73 problem imported into the trial.

Step four: apply the therapist-effects figure. In Trial B, the same clinicians delivered both arms; that design choice partly controls for therapist effects, which is a virtue. In Trial A, clinicians delivered only the active condition, so any between-therapist differences load entirely onto the active arm's outcome. The review reporting that therapists accounted for about 8.6% of outcome variance across 27 treatment groups [4] gives that design detail a number to sit next to. Neither trial is thereby invalid; but the reader can now say exactly what each result means and what it does not.
lessons.question: A fictional guideline states: 'Therapy X has a large effect size of 0.9 in randomised trials, so it should be preferred to Therapy Y, whose trials report 0.4.' Using this lesson's sources, what is the strongest objection?
lessons.answer: Effect sizes from trials with different control conditions measure different quantities, so the comparison is uninterpretable unless the comparators, delivery conditions and outcome measures are matched; a therapy trialled against a waiting list is not comparable to one trialled against an active control, and therapist effects add a clinician-specific component to each estimate.
lessons.distractor: The comparison is valid because both figures are standardised effect sizes derived from randomised trials, and standardisation exists precisely to make results from different studies comparable.
lessons.correction: Standardisation makes units comparable, not comparisons. The network meta-analysis found that effect estimates for the same therapy differed substantively depending on whether the comparator was a waiting list, no treatment, or a psychological placebo, and reported that no-treatment exceeded waiting list with an odds ratio of 2.9 for response [2]; a therapy tested against a waiting list therefore carries an inflated apparent effect relative to the same therapy tested against an active control. Therapist effects compound it: about 8.6% of outcome variance across 27 treatment groups was attributable to the individual clinician [4], so part of any headline effect is a property of the trial's staff. Munder's finding that the mean allegiance-outcome association was r = .262 and that allegiance to the allegiance hypothesis moderated it [3] adds a further reason to compare designs before comparing numbers. The defensible practice is to compare effect sizes only within matched comparisons, and otherwise to compare the trials' structures: populations, comparators, outcome measures, delivery, and allegiance.

depth.definitions:
Non-specific factors: features of treatment not tied to a specified technique — attention, expectancy, structure, the therapeutic relationship, the act of being assessed — sometimes called common factors by those who argue they are the treatment rather than contamination. Placebo response: improvement in the control arm of a trial of an active intervention, arising from expectancy, natural course, regression to the mean, and the effects of assessment. Nocebo: worsening attributable to negative expectation; the descriptive claim that waiting lists may act this way is a hypothesis from one network meta-analysis [2]. Waiting list, no treatment, and psychological placebo: three distinct comparators whose effects differ [2]. Active control: a comparator intended to match non-specific elements while omitting the specific technique. Therapist effects: variance in outcome attributable to the individual clinician, estimated at about 8.6% across 27 treatment groups [4]. Researcher allegiance: the association between researchers' preferences for a treatment and the effects reported for it, summarised meta-analytically at r = .262 across 30 meta-analyses [3]. Blinding: structurally harder in psychotherapy than in trials of medication, because participants and therapists know what they are receiving; assessor blinding is the usual partial remedy.

Prerequisite: lesson 76 for average effects and comparators, lesson 77 for reporting bias and appraisal tools, and lesson 73 for measurement and interpretability, which is what the placebo-response discussion partly is.
depth.mechanism:
Four mechanisms explain why the control arm shapes the result so much, and they have different remedies.

Mechanism one: subtraction of non-specific improvement. If the control condition produces improvement, the observed difference is the increment over that improvement. A waiting list may produce little; an active control with the same number of appointments produces substantially more; hence the same therapy can report very different effects. There is no remedy that makes the two comparable — the honest solution is to specify which comparison a given effect estimate comes from and never to compare across them.

Mechanism two: differential attrition and disappointment. People assigned to conditions they perceive as less desirable leave trials, and attrition is rarely symmetric across arms, which changes the analysed populations in ways that can be consistent with either inflation or deflation of the estimate. This is one of the domains that structured risk-of-bias assessment addresses trial by trial, and the reason the Furukawa authors could not run their planned restriction to high-quality studies is that so few trials met the bar [2].

Mechanism three: the clinician as an unmeasured variable. If 8.6% of outcome variance is attributable to the individual therapist [4], then a trial's effect is partly an estimate of its staff, and the transfer to a service depends on whether the service can hire, train, supervise and retain comparable staff. This is why fidelity monitoring is not administrative decoration: it is an attempt to keep the delivered intervention constant across people and settings.

Mechanism four: expectancy written into both participants and assessors. When participants know which arm they are in and outcomes are collected by people who may also know, the estimate incorporates expectations at both ends. Blinding of assessors, use of pre-registered objective outcomes, and independent outcome adjudication reduce but do not remove it, and in psychological treatment the participant cannot be blinded at all. This is the structural reason the field's effect sizes require the additional scrutiny this unit is teaching.

One further mechanism belongs here because it explains the debate itself: allegiance. Munder's synthesis found a moderate, robust association between researchers' allegiance and reported effects [3], and found that allegiance to the allegiance hypothesis moderated it. Both halves matter: the association is real enough to adjust your reading for, and researchers' own views about that association are part of the phenomenon.
depth.secondExample:
A contrasting case from medication trials, chosen because the comparator is chemically well matched and yet the same reasoning still applies.

A fictional trial compares an active compound against an identical-looking tablet with no active ingredient, in people with moderate symptoms. This is the strongest control design available: participants cannot distinguish arms, so expectancy is roughly matched, and any difference is attributable to the compound plus its side-effect profile, which is not nothing — participants who notice side effects may infer they are in the active arm, a phenomenon known as partial unblinding, which itself can affect reporting.

Two differences from the psychotherapy case are worth extracting. First, because the comparator is matched, the trial's effect is a smaller, more specific quantity than a trial against no treatment: it answers 'does the compound add over expectancy and the trial's own structure?', not 'is this better than nothing?' The Kirsch analysis lives inside exactly that comparison, and its finding that the difference grows with severity but remains small even at very severe levels [1] is a statement about the matched comparison, not about untreated illness. Second, the reported difference of 1.80 points on a clinician-rated scale must be interpreted using lesson 73's vocabulary: which threshold counts as clinically significant is a convention, and the threshold itself is contested.

Now the comparison that completes the picture. In the psychological therapy case, a trial against an active control reduced the measured increment; in the medication case, the matched placebo does the same job by design. Both therefore produce smaller estimates than their non-matched counterparts, and neither is thereby 'more honest'. They are simply different questions: effectiveness relative to available alternatives is usually the decision-relevant question for a service, and specific efficacy relative to a matched control is the decision-relevant question for a mechanism claim. The transferable skill is to name the comparison before reading the number, and to be suspicious of any summary that presents a single effect size as though the comparator were incidental. This is also the discipline GRADE imposes by rating outcomes for a stated comparison: the certainty rating is about that comparison, not about the treatment in the abstract.
depth.mistake:
Misconception one: that the placebo or control response is simply the absence of treatment, so the difference equals the treatment's effect. Control conditions differ measurably in what they produce — the network meta-analysis found substantively different estimates depending on whether the comparator was a waiting list, no treatment or a psychological placebo, with an odds ratio of 2.9 for response comparing no treatment with waiting list [2] — and a waiting list is not nothing, as the nocebo framing suggests. Its evidential status is provisional, given the authors' own inability to restrict analysis to high-quality trials or to preserve the finding after adjustment for publication bias [2].

Misconception two: that non-specific factors are a polite word for cheating, so a trial with a large non-specific component is fraudulent. They are the unavoidable context of any treatment: hope, attention, structure and expectation accompany every clinical encounter. The question is never whether they exist but whether a study has measured the specific increment over them, and whether the claim being made is about the increment or about the whole package.

Misconception three: that therapist effects are a minor nuisance. Eight-point-six percent of outcome variance across 27 treatment groups is substantial [4], and it is larger than many specific treatment contrasts in the same literature; if it is ignored, a service can adopt a protocol that performed well because of who delivered it and observe different results. Allegiance compounds the same problem at the level of the research team [3], and the fact that belief in the allegiance hypothesis moderated the association is the sharpest illustration available that no one in this system, reader included, is outside it.

Diagnostic correction: whenever you read 'Treatment X is effective', finish the sentence — 'compared with what, delivered by whom, to whom, and measured how?' Four answers are required, and any effect size quoted without them is incomplete in a way that matters for decisions.
depth.application:
Nonblocking task. A fictional commissioner is shown two trials of the same therapy and one service report. Trial 1: therapy versus waiting list, effect size 0.85, 60% of completers followed up, therapists supervised weekly by the therapy's developers, outcome self-report. Trial 2: therapy versus active control, effect size 0.25, 92% followed up, therapists supervised monthly by a service supervisor, outcome independent assessor rating plus self-report. Service report: outcomes after two years of routine delivery, no control group, mean score improvement that exceeds trial 2's effect.

Write a 200-word briefing that: states which trial answers which question; identifies two features of trial 1 that would make you cautious about its effect estimate; and explains what the service report can and cannot show. Finish with one sentence on what you would measure before adopting the therapy service-wide.

Model briefing. Trial 1 answers whether therapy beats waiting for this population, and its larger effect size partly reflects that comparison; trial 2 answers whether the specific package adds over matched non-specific care, and is the more relevant estimate for a service already able to offer supportive contact. Cautions about trial 1: the comparator is a waiting list, which the depression network meta-analysis suggests may behave as a nocebo rather than an inert baseline, and effect estimates in that analysis differed substantively by comparator type [2]; follow-up covered only 60% of completers, uneven attrition between arms can move estimates in either direction and is one of the domains structured risk-of-bias assessment examines; add, if asked for a third, that supervision by the developers introduces an allegiance component, and allegiance shows a moderate mean association with reported effects, r = .262, itself moderated by researchers' belief in it [3]. What the service report shows: change over time in people who attended, and therefore a mixture of treatment effect, regression to the mean, spontaneous fluctuation and expectancy; without a comparison it cannot separate them. One measurement before adopting service-wide: therapist effects, by tracking outcome variation across clinicians, because about 8.6% of outcome variance in the review evidence sat with the individual therapist [4], and that is what fidelity and supervision are supposed to hold constant.

Rubric: 1 point for correctly assigning each trial to its question; 1 for two specific cautions tied to design rather than general scepticism; 1 for distinguishing change over time from an effect; 1 for measuring something that addresses delivery (therapist variation, fidelity, supervision) rather than only patient outcomes. Three or four points indicates that comparators and delivery are being treated as part of the effect.
depth.summary:
An effect size is a difference, and this lesson examined the subtrahend: the control condition, the expectancy and attention bound up with any clinical encounter, and the person delivering the treatment. The matched comparison in the FDA analysis leaves a drug-placebo difference that grows with severity but remains small even in severe depression, against a contested clinical-significance threshold [1]. The depression network meta-analysis shows that comparators are not interchangeable and that a waiting list may be worse than nothing, while honestly recording that its own findings are provisional [2]. Therapist effects account for about 8.6% of outcome variance across 27 treatment groups [4], and researcher allegiance shows a moderate, robust association with reported effects across 30 meta-analyses [3].

Transfer: this closes the evidence-reading sequence. The next lesson moves from the trial to the system — the level at which access, continuity, workforce and social conditions determine who is even in the trials, and what a service change can plausibly achieve.

readings.title: Kirsch, I. et al. (2008), 'Initial Severity and Antidepressant Benefits: A Meta-Analysis of Data Submitted to the Food and Drug Administration', PLoS Medicine 5(2):e45
readings.note: Read the abstract and the analysis of initial severity, including the finding that drug-placebo differences rise with severity but are relatively small even for severely depressed patients, and the comparison between the mean 1.80-point difference on the Hamilton scale and the 3-point threshold for clinical significance that the paper cites. This pack does not endorse a prescribing conclusion and takes no position on what any individual should be offered; read the paper for its method and read the critical replies it attracted before drawing a clinical conclusion, because both the severity analysis and the interpretation of the placebo response are contested in the literature.

readings.title: Furukawa, T. A. et al. (2014), 'Waiting list may be a nocebo condition in psychotherapy trials: a contribution from network meta-analysis', Acta Psychiatrica Scandinavica 130(3):181-192 — PubMed record
readings.note: Read the abstract: 49 randomised controlled trials with 2,730 participants comparing waiting list, no treatment, psychological placebo and cognitive behavioural therapy, substantively different effect estimates by control condition, an odds ratio of 2.9 (95% CI 1.3 to 5.7) for response comparing no treatment with waiting list, and the authors' caveats that evidence quality including publication bias was less than ideal, that no preplanned sensitivity analysis restricted to high-quality studies could be conducted, and that the significant differences did not survive post hoc adjustment for publication bias. Access caveat: PubMed serves scripted clients a reduced version of the record while rendering normally in a browser, so open this in a browser; the publisher's version of the article is behind a paywall.

readings.title: Munder, T., Brütsch, O., Leonhart, R., Gerger, H. & Barth, J. (2013), 'Researcher allegiance in psychotherapy outcome research: an overview of reviews', Clinical Psychology Review 33(4):501-511 — PubMed record
readings.note: Read the abstract for the meta-meta-analysis: thirty meta-analyses, mean allegiance-outcome association r = .262 (p = .002, I² = 28.98%), robustness across moderators, and the finding that allegiance towards the allegiance-bias hypothesis moderated the association. Access caveat as above: browser required, publisher version paywalled. Treat the association as evidence about the research literature's properties, and note that the two independent source types here (a single network meta-analysis and an overview of meta-analyses) differ in strength of evidence.

readings.title: Johns, R. G., Barkham, M., Kellett, S. & Saxon, D. (2019), 'A systematic review of therapist effects: A critical narrative update and refinement to Baldwin and Imel's (2013) review' (author's copy, White Rose eprint repository)
readings.note: Read the introduction and methods for how therapist effects are estimated from outcome data, and the section reporting magnitudes: therapists accounted for an average of 8.6% of outcome variance across 27 treatment groups, alongside Wampold's earlier estimate of approximately 8%. Read the authors' critical discussion of the limitations of the evidence, including the difficulty of separating therapist effects from case-mix and from measurement error. Access caveat: this is the author's accepted version in an institutional repository; the journal version may differ in pagination.

visual.title: Seven labelled elements of a comparison, and what each contributes to the measured effect
visual.description: A decomposition diagram of a reported treatment effect, showing that the number is a difference between two conditions whose contents determine its size.
steps: Element 1 — The specific technique: what the intervention adds over everything else in the room. Contributes the increment that a mechanism claim is about.
Element 2 — Attention and structure: appointments, regularity, contact with an interested person, monitoring. Present in most active arms and, in matched designs, in the control arm too.
Element 3 — Expectancy and hope: participant and clinician beliefs about the arm assigned. Reduced by blinding where possible, and structurally unmatched in psychological treatment.

Element 4 — Natural course and regression to the mean: improvement that occurs regardless of treatment, especially when people enter studies at their worst. Larger in episodic conditions and at high baseline severity.
Element 5 — Measurement reactivity: change in what a scale captures because measurement is happening (lesson 73). Affects both arms, and differently if assessment is unblinded.

Element 6 — The clinician: about 8.6% of outcome variance across 27 treatment groups was attributable to the individual therapist. Partly controlled in designs where the same clinicians deliver all arms.

Element 7 — The comparator's own content: waiting list, no treatment, psychological placebo, matched pill, or active control. The choice changes effect estimates substantively, and it defines the question the effect size answers.

lessons.title: Systems reasoning: how services and conditions shape outcomes
lessons.explanation:
Everything so far has been about evidence. This lesson changes the unit of analysis from the intervention to the system, because at population level the largest determinants of what happens to people with mental health conditions are not differences in technique but who can reach a service, what the service can offer, and what conditions surround the person. Education only; no service or treatment is recommended here for anyone.

Begin with the scale and the gaps, from WHO's 2022 world mental health report. The report states that about one in eight people in the world live with a mental disorder; that in 2019 an estimated 970 million people globally were living with a mental disorder, 82% of whom were in low- and middle-income countries; that 71% of people with psychosis do not receive mental health services; and that, on average, 2% of health budgets go to mental health [1]. Its summary framing is worth carrying as a single phrase: mental health needs are widespread, undertreated and under-resourced [1]. Do the arithmetic once so the numbers become real: 82% of 970 million is about 795 million people in low- and middle-income countries alone, and if 71% of people with psychosis are not in contact with services, then in any population of 1,000 people with psychosis, roughly 710 are outside the service [1]. Any clinical trial effect size is a statement about the remaining 290.

For country-level service capacity, WHO's Mental Health Atlas is the reference collection: it publishes country profiles covering governance, financing, workforce and service availability, and it is the place to look up a specific country's position rather than reasoning from a global average [2]. Two cautions attend its use. Figures are collected periodically rather than continuously, so they lag; and definitions of categories such as 'mental health professional' and 'inpatient bed' vary between countries, so cross-country comparisons require reading the definitions before the numbers.

Now the design question: what can a service do? A narrative synthesis of community-based models of care for people with persistent and complex mental health needs makes an argument worth extracting. It notes that many people living with severe or persistent conditions experience coercive, traumatic or discriminatory treatment, which may lead to reluctance to engage with support; that dissatisfaction with treatment and poor recovery outcomes may relate to limited treatment options, including lack of access to evidence-based psychosocial models of care; and that both inpatient and community-based models have a role in achieving clinical, functional and personal recovery outcomes, which is why it focuses on community models given the increased emphasis on community-based care [3]. It also concludes that involvement of people with lived experience in designing, delivering, implementing and researching models of care is needed to make them relevant to individual recovery outcomes [3].

Then the conditions surrounding the person, which are not background. A review in Science by economists and a psychiatrist synthesises the evidence for what they describe as a bidirectional causal relationship between poverty and common mental illnesses, depression and anxiety, and examines the mechanisms; it reports that people with the lowest incomes are typically 1.5 to 3 times more likely than the rich to experience depression or anxiety, and it reviews evidence on interventions including cash support and low-cost therapeutic interventions [4]. Two implications for systems reasoning. First, an intervention evaluated in a trial population that excludes people in severe material hardship may not behave the same way in a service whose users are largely in that situation — which is a generalisability question of the same kind lesson 76 raised about risk-based heterogeneity. Second, a service-level strategy that ignores material conditions is selecting one mechanism of ill health and hoping it dominates, which is a testable assumption rather than a neutral design choice.

Systems have characteristic failure modes, and knowing them by name is the practical skill of this lesson. Substitution: an intervention in one place displaces rather than replaces another, so the measured improvement in one setting is partly the deterioration of another — which is why counts of people placed outside their own area matter as a service metric rather than an administrative detail [5]. Threshold shifting: when demand exceeds capacity, the entry threshold moves, and the apparent severity of the caseload changes without any change in the population; this can make a service look more efficient while simply excluding more people, and it is why denominators and referral rates belong next to outcome figures. Target gaming: any measure used for accountability becomes a measure people manage, which is the service-level version of the researcher degrees of freedom in lesson 75. Inequity: who is referred, who attends, who completes, and who is discharged without follow-up are all distributional facts that summary means conceal. And condition-dependence: a service's outcomes depend on staffing, supervision and caseload, so a model that works at one staffing level is not the same intervention at another — the fidelity and therapist-effects problem of lesson 78, rescaled.

The reasoning discipline to take away: for any claim about a service, ask who is in the denominator, what the comparison is, what else changed at the same time, and whether the outcome is the one the people using the service would choose. Those four questions are the systems equivalent of prior odds, power, pre-specification and certainty.
lessons.example:
Worked reasoning on a fictional service reform, chosen because reforms usually work partly and are usually reported as though they worked wholly.

The reform: a mental health trust closes an inpatient ward and funds a crisis home-treatment team, on the grounds that home treatment is better for recovery and cheaper. Eighteen months later it reports that average length of stay for people still admitted has fallen and that patient satisfaction with home treatment is high, and declares the reform a success.

Step one: identify the claim precisely. 'Success' here bundles at least four claims: better outcomes for people who would previously have been admitted, no worse outcomes for people who are now not admitted, no shift of burden onto families, and lower cost. Each needs its own evidence, and the reported figures address none of them directly — length of stay among those still admitted is a statement about a shrinking group, and satisfaction with a new service is measured among the people who chose to use it.

Step two: look for substitution. If people who would have been admitted are now treated at home, and some of them deteriorate, the deterioration appears in readmission data, in emergency department presentations, in out-of-area placements, or in the criminal justice system — which is exactly why placement outside the local area is tracked as a national statistic in England [5]. Substitution is the most common way a service reform improves one number while leaving the total unchanged or worse, and it is invisible unless all the settings that could absorb the displaced demand are measured.

Step three: look for threshold shifting. Closing beds raises the bar for admission. Lower average length of stay among admitted patients is then partly a compositional change: the people now admitted are a more selected, and probably less complex, group. That does not make the figure wrong; it makes it uninterpretable without the denominator and without the admission threshold, which is why referral rates, bed occupancy and refused admissions belong in the same report.

Step four: check whether the outcome is the one service users would choose. The community models review argues that involvement of people with lived experience in designing, delivering and researching models of care is needed for relevance to individual recovery outcomes [3], which is a statement about whose judgement defines success. Satisfaction among people who accepted home treatment is one input; outcomes for people who declined it, or who were admitted anyway, are others, and the review's observation about reluctance to engage following coercive or discriminatory experiences suggests some of the relevant experience is invisible to a satisfaction survey [3].

Step five: put the reform in the population frame. Global figures say that most people who need services never reach them and that budgets are small [1]; a reform that redistributes the budget for the few already in contact may improve their care or degrade it, but it cannot by itself change that larger pattern. Denying this is not a criticism of the reform; it is a limit on what any single service change can be shown to achieve. The defensible summary of this reform after eighteen months: home treatment is acceptable to those who chose it; the effect on outcomes for the displaced group is unknown; the effect on families is unmeasured; and the cost claim requires counting the substitute settings, not the closed ward.
lessons.question: A fictional health board reports: 'After introducing a new community team, admissions fell by 22%, so the team prevented 22% of admissions.' Which correction is best supported by this lesson's material?
lessons.answer: A fall in admissions in one setting is a redistribution of activity until proven otherwise: displaced demand may appear in other settings, the admission threshold may have shifted, and the comparison requires a counterfactual, so the claim needs counts across all potentially substitute settings and a denominator before it can be attributed to the team.
lessons.distractor: The claim is valid because admissions are an objective, routinely collected measure that is not susceptible to recording bias, unlike satisfaction or symptom scores.
lessons.correction: Routine measures are objective in their recording and not in their meaning; what they mean depends on what else happened, which is exactly what the correction states. Two further points from the lesson sharpen it. First, substitution is a named and measured phenomenon — placements outside a provider's own area are collected as a national statistic in England precisely because activity can move between settings rather than disappearing [5]. Second, the denominator: if the board serves a growing population, or if the new team operates alongside a lower acceptance threshold, the admission rate and the admission count can move in different directions, and only one of them is being reported. A defensible version of the claim would specify the comparator period, the population served, all alternate destinations for displaced demand, and the criteria for admission in each period; without those, the 22% is a description of one number changing.

depth.definitions:
System or service-level reasoning: analysis in which the unit is a service, a catchment or a population rather than an individual, and in which access, continuity, capacity and social conditions are treated as causal variables. Treatment gap: the proportion of people with a condition who are not receiving care; WHO's report puts it at 71% for people with psychosis [1]. Continuity of care: the extent to which a person experiences a coherent, connected sequence of care rather than disconnected episodes; a service property that individual-level trials cannot capture. Substitution: displacement of activity from one setting to another, which can make a local improvement look like a net gain. Threshold shifting: change in entry criteria as capacity changes, altering the case mix and thus any average computed over it. Out-of-area placement: admitting someone outside their local provider's area, used here as an example of a substitute destination that official statistics track [5]. Fidelity: the extent to which a service delivers the intervention as specified; in psychological treatment this depends on staffing, training, supervision and caseload, and it interacts with therapist effects (lesson 78). Social determinants: material and social conditions that causally influence mental health, summarised here through the bidirectional relationship between poverty and depression and anxiety [4].

Prerequisite: lessons 76-78 for treatment evidence, comparators and delivery; lesson 53, from the earlier level, for levels of care and escalation.
depth.mechanism:
Why do system-level facts dominate individual-level ones, and what follows for reasoning?

Mechanism one: selection into care. Trials recruit people who reach services, consent to study, and meet criteria. If 71% of people with psychosis never reach mental health services [1], then the evidence base describes the minority who do, and its generalisability to everyone with the condition is an assumption rather than a finding. The same logic applies locally: a service's outcome data describes its attenders, and its effect on the population it is nominally responsible for depends on how many people it never sees.

Mechanism two: capacity determines case mix. When demand exceeds supply, something gives: waiting times rise, thresholds rise, or clinicians reduce time per person. Any of these changes who is in the treated group, so service averages move for reasons unrelated to clinical skill. This is the mechanism behind threshold shifting, and it is why a service that reports improving outcomes during a period of rising demand deserves a question rather than a congratulations or a suspicion.

Mechanism three: continuity as a treatment ingredient. Fragmented care has costs: repeated assessments, lost history, delayed recognition of change, and a lower chance that anything learned in one episode informs the next. The community models review's point that dissatisfaction and poor recovery outcomes may relate to limited treatment options and lack of access to evidence-based psychosocial care [3] is a statement about what a system offers, not about what a clinician does in a room.

Mechanism four: material conditions. The economic review summarises evidence that poverty and common mental illness are causally related in both directions, with people on the lowest incomes typically 1.5 to 3 times more likely to experience depression or anxiety, and reviews interventions including cash support alongside therapeutic ones [4]. This matters for interpretation in both directions: a clinical intervention may be swamped by conditions it cannot alter, and a policy intervention may change mental health outcomes without touching the clinical system.

Mechanism five: measurement as an intervention. Once a number is used for accountability, it is managed. Some of that management is legitimate improvement; some is definitional drift, reclassification, or shifting activity across boundaries where the measure does not reach. The systems response is not to abandon measurement but to insist on several measures across settings and to treat any single figure as a proxy, which is the service-level analogue of the appraisal discipline in lesson 77.
depth.secondExample:
A contrasting case at the smallest possible scale, in which the same systems reasoning applies to one clinician's week — useful because it shows that this is a way of thinking rather than a policy topic.

A fictional community psychiatric nurse has 120 people on her caseload and eight hours of scheduled contact per day less an hour of documentation, travel and supervision. She has just been asked to add a newly evidenced relapse-prevention intervention requiring twelve hourly sessions over three months to everyone on her caseload with a psychosis diagnosis, of whom there are 40.

Do the arithmetic. Twelve sessions times 40 people is 480 hours over three months, which is roughly 37 hours a week of that intervention alone, against a working week of about 37-40 hours in total including travel and documentation. The intervention cannot be delivered as specified to that caseload by that service. Now list the realistic responses, because this is where systems reasoning becomes concrete. Substitution: deliver it to some and something else stops. Threshold shifting: deliver it only to those judged most likely to benefit, which is a defensible clinical choice and also a rationing decision that should be named rather than buried. Fidelity drift: deliver a shortened version and report it as the intervention, which is the mechanism by which trial effects vanish on implementation, and the reason fidelity measurement exists (lesson 78). Workforce change: recruit or retrain, which is a service-level decision with a lead time usually exceeding the political cycle. And honest reporting: state that the intervention is available to a defined subgroup and describe who is excluded, which is what lets the next person reason about coverage.

Notice what did not happen in that reasoning: nobody needed to know whether the intervention works. That question was settled by the trial evidence, with all the qualifications of lessons 76 to 78. The system question is whether the intervention can be delivered, to whom, at what cost to what else, and how that will be recorded — and it is the question that determines whether the trial's effect ever reaches a person. The transferable comparison with the ward-closure example: both concern capacity and substitution; the only difference is the size of the bookkeeping.
depth.mistake:
Misconception one: that population-level gaps are somebody else's subject. The treatment-gap figures are not background to clinical work; they determine what a trial's effect size applies to. A 71% gap between people with psychosis and service contact [1] means that clinical evidence describes a minority of the affected population, so generalisation is an empirical question rather than an assumption.

Misconception two: that a service reform's local improvement is evidence of a net improvement. Substitution and threshold shifting can produce improvement in one measured setting while total activity or total suffering is unchanged, or worse; the reason out-of-area placements are tracked as a statistic is that displaced need has to go somewhere [5]. The correction is to count all the settings that can absorb displaced demand before attributing an effect.

Misconception three: that a randomised trial's result transfers to a service automatically. Delivery conditions — staffing, supervision, caseload, fidelity — are part of the intervention, as the therapist-effects evidence in lesson 78 shows; and the community models review argues explicitly that implementation should involve people with lived experience if the models are to be relevant to recovery outcomes [3]. A service that reproduces a protocol with a third of the staffing has not reproduced the intervention.

Misconception four: that acknowledging social determinants makes clinical work pointless. The economic review reports causal influence in both directions and reviews interventions including cash support as well as low-cost therapeutic ones [4]; the point is that clinical and social interventions operate on different parts of the same system, not that one displaces the other.

Diagnostic correction: when a service claim is made, ask for four things — the denominator and the referral rate, all settings where displaced activity could appear, the comparison and what else changed at the same time, and whether the outcome was chosen with the people using the service.
depth.application:
Nonblocking task. You are given a fictional package: (a) a system with 40,000 adults in the catchment; (b) WHO-type figures indicating that about one in eight people live with a mental disorder [1]; (c) a specialist service with 6 full-time clinicians, each able to carry an active caseload of 60; (d) a proposed new intervention requiring 10 sessions per person, delivered once every two weeks. Write a 200-word capacity analysis: how many people the catchment's prevalence implies; what the service can currently carry; how many people the new intervention could reach at full delivery; and one honest statement of what the remaining people are offered instead.

Model response. Expected number with a mental disorder: 40,000 / 8 = 5,000 adults. Service capacity: 6 clinicians x 60 active cases = 360 people in current contact, or 7.2% of those 5,000 — consistent in order of magnitude with the WHO report's treatment-gap figures, which describe most need as unmet [1]. Intervention reach: 10 sessions each fortnight covers 20 weeks per person. Base it on available clinician hours rather than caseload alone: assuming 6 clinicians deliver 3 intervention sessions a day each for 200 working days, that is 6 x 3 x 200 = 3,600 sessions a year, or 360 people at 10 sessions each — that is, the intervention at full delivery would consume the service's entire capacity, leaving nothing for anything else. A more realistic allocation of a fifth of clinician time gives 72 people a year, or about 1.4% of the 5,000, and roughly 20% of current service users. Remaining people: those not selected are offered the service's existing provision, which after the reallocation is thinner than before; the honest statement is that the intervention is available to a defined subgroup, that selection is by criteria the service must state and defend, and that the rest receive less than they did.

Rubric: 1 point for computing prevalence and capacity correctly and labelling assumptions; 1 point for noticing that the intervention competes with existing provision rather than adding to it; 1 point for expressing reach as a proportion of need rather than as a count; 1 point for naming the selection rule and who is excluded. Three or four points indicates that capacity, substitution and coverage are being reasoned together; two or fewer usually means the intervention has been considered without its opportunity cost.
depth.summary:
Services and conditions set the frame within which all the trial evidence of the previous lessons operates. WHO's report supplies the order of magnitude — about one in eight people living with a mental disorder, 970 million in 2019 with 82% in low- and middle-income countries, 71% of people with psychosis outside mental health services, and about 2% of health budgets for mental health [1] — and the Atlas is the reference collection for country-level workforce and service data, to be read with attention to definitions and to collection dates [2]. What a service can offer determines who benefits: community models have an argued role alongside inpatient care, and their relevance to recovery depends on involving people with lived experience [3]. Material conditions are causal, not decorative: poverty and common mental illness are related in both directions, with the lowest-income groups typically 1.5 to 3 times more likely to experience depression or anxiety [4]. And activity displaced by a service change has to go somewhere, which is why substitute destinations are measured [5].

Transfer: the final lesson asks you to assemble everything in this level into one appraisal of a claim, and to write down what remains unknown. That discipline — provenance, comparison, measurement, delivery, system, unknown — is the whole level in six words.
