readings.note: Read the background for the argument used here — that people living with severe or persistent conditions experience coercion, trauma and discrimination which can reduce engagement, that dissatisfaction and poor recovery outcomes may relate to limited treatment options including lack of access to evidence-based psychosocial care, and that both inpatient and community models have roles in achieving clinical, functional and personal recovery. Read the conclusions for the call to involve people with lived experience in design, delivery, implementation and research. This is a narrative synthesis, which is a weaker design than a systematic review with meta-analysis; read it for the range of models and their stated gaps.

readings.title: Ridley, M., Rao, G., Schilbach, F. & Patel, V. (2020), 'Poverty, depression, and anxiety: Causal evidence and mechanisms', Science 370(6522):eaay0214 (author copy via MIT Economics)
readings.note: Read the abstract and the review for the claim that recent research has established a bidirectional causal relationship between poverty and mental illness, for the prevalence gradient (people with the lowest incomes typically 1.5 to 3 times more likely to experience depression or anxiety), for the mechanisms discussed, and for the interventions reviewed, including cash support and low-cost therapeutic interventions. Access caveat: this link is an author copy hosted by MIT; the version of record is in Science and may be behind a paywall. Note that this is an economic review written by economists with a psychiatrist co-author; its causal language rests on designs such as cash transfer studies, which should be read for their own limitations.

readings.title: NHS England / GOV.UK official statistics, 'Out of Area Placements in Mental Health Services' (monthly collection)
readings.note: An example of a service metric that exists precisely because activity can be displaced between settings: adult acute mental health patients treated outside their provider's own area. Read the background and methodology sections for what the collection records and its stated limitations, and use the data tables for figures rather than the summary page, which is brief. Access note: this is a national administrative collection with its own definitions and reporting caveats, not a research study; treat it as a measurement of service activity, and check the definitions before comparing periods.

visual.title: Six labelled levels from population need to individual contact, with the filter operating at each
visual.description: A funnel diagram showing how a population's need narrows to the people a service actually treats, naming at each level what determines the narrowing and what a service can and cannot control.
steps: Level 1 — Population need: WHO estimates about one in eight people live with a mental disorder; in 2019 about 970 million people, 82% of them in low- and middle-income countries. Nothing here is under a service's control.

Level 2 — Recognised need and help-seeking: stigma, prior coercive or discriminatory experiences, knowledge and cost determine whether anyone tries to reach care. Services influence this only indirectly, through reputation, accessibility and rights practice.
Level 3 — Referral and acceptance: GP or self-referral meets a service threshold. Threshold shifting at this level changes the case mix and therefore every average computed downstream.

Level 4 — Capacity and delivery: staffing, caseloads and supervision determine what can actually be delivered and with what fidelity; about 71% of people with psychosis do not receive mental health services, so this level is where most need is lost.
Level 5 — Continuity over time: whether care is a sequence or a series of disconnected episodes. Fragmentation contributes to poor recovery outcomes and to reluctance to re-engage.

Level 6 — Substituted settings: when care moves, activity appears elsewhere — readmission, emergency departments, out-of-area placements, families, criminal justice. Counting only the primary setting hides the shift.

lessons.title: Capstone: adjudicating a claim — provenance, comparison, measurement, delivery, system, unknown
lessons.explanation:
This level began with describing an experience and ends with a procedure for deciding how much weight a claim about mental health deserves. This capstone assembles the procedure and is explicit about what it cannot do. Education only: it is not a method for diagnosing a person, it is not treatment advice, and completing it — or answering the quiz items that follow — is not evidence of clinical competence. Judgements about an individual's care belong to a qualified clinician who knows that person, and nothing in this pack substitutes for that.

The procedure has six questions, asked in order, and each one exists because of a specific failure it catches.

One, what exactly is being claimed? Restate it as a sentence with a population, a comparator, an outcome and a time frame. Most disagreements in this field dissolve at this step, because a claim that was never specified cannot be checked. A service target, a mechanism story, a prediction and an average effect are four different claims, and lesson 76 showed how often they are confused.

Two, what kind of evidence is this, and where does it come from? Descriptive accounts, group comparisons, randomised trials, syntheses and administrative statistics have different strengths, and the first question about any of them is provenance: who collected it, on whom, and with what incentives. Where a regulator's or funder's complete trial record exists, it is the better source for a question about the literature as a whole, because the published record is a selected sample of it [1].

Three, how was it measured? Ask what the instrument actually codes, whether it behaves comparably across the groups being compared, how much change it can detect beyond noise, and what change the people involved would consider meaningful. Lesson 73 supplied the vocabulary: consistency, structure, invariance, and interpretability are separate claims, and no single coefficient settles more than one of them.

Four, what was compared, and who delivered it? An effect is a difference, and the control condition is part of it — a waiting list, a no-treatment arm, a psychological placebo and an active control produce substantively different estimates — while the individual clinician accounts for a measurable share of outcome variance, so a result is partly a statement about the trial's staff and supervision. Where a paper reports a treatment effect, the appraisal must state the comparator and the delivery conditions, not just the number.

Five, what does the wider literature say about this body of evidence? Registration status and completeness, evidence of selective reporting, whether the synthesis could assess small-study effects at all, and a certainty rating with named reasons for rating down. The corrective here is structural rather than moral: practices improved over time in the antidepressant literature, with transparent reporting rising from 11% to 47% between cohorts, and remained asymmetric, with 100% of positive trials transparently reported against 47% of negative ones [1]. The certainty rating is a judgement made against explicit criteria rather than a measurement, and its authors say so [2].

Six, in what system does this claim have to be true? Who is excluded from the evidence, what setting would absorb displaced activity, and what is the denominator. Global figures — about one in eight people living with a mental disorder, and 71% of people with psychosis not in contact with services — describe the population the evidence has to serve, and they are far larger than any within-service effect [3].

Then the last part, which is what separates an appraisal from a verdict: write the uncertainty down. Three things belong in that record. Provenance: for each load-bearing claim, where it came from and how strong the source is, including whether the source is one of the contested ones. Unknowns: the specific quantities whose absence bounds the conclusion, phrased so that someone could supply them — the outcome base rate in a comparable population, the proportion above a threshold who reach the outcome, the comparator-matched effect. Revision conditions: what would change your conclusion, stated in advance, so that later evidence can do its work rather than being absorbed as confirmation. A conclusion written this way is more useful than a confident one, because the next reader can move it.

One caution about this procedure as a whole. It can be performed as ritual: six headings, each completed with a sentence that changes nothing. The test of whether an appraisal has done work is whether the conclusion is weaker, narrower or differently worded than the claim it examined. If a claim passes all six questions unmodified, either it was strong to begin with — rarer than it appears — or the appraisal was decoration.
lessons.example:
A worked appraisal of a fictional composite claim, written in the form this lesson recommends. The claim: 'A new blended digital and face-to-face therapy for depression is more effective than usual care and should be commissioned.'

One, the claim restated. For adults with moderate depression in a community service, compared with usual care, a blended programme improves depressive symptoms and functioning over twelve months, sufficiently to justify commissioning. Note that four things are bundled: superiority over usual care, improvement in two different outcomes, persistence to twelve months, and a decision about commissioning. The last does not follow from the first three at all, because it also depends on cost, workforce, and what would be displaced.

Two, the evidence and its provenance. Suppose the assertion rests on one two-site randomised trial of 240 people, funded and analysed by the programme's developer, and a service evaluation from a pilot site that reported high satisfaction. Provenance questions follow immediately: only one trial, a developer interest, and a satisfaction-based service report, which cannot estimate an effect without a comparison. Under the reporting-bias framework, a single published trial with a positive result is exactly the kind of evidence whose published record improved least: in the antidepressant comparison, transparency was complete for positive trials and about half for negative ones [1].

Three, measurement. If the primary outcome was a self-report symptom scale, the appraisal needs the scale's behaviour across the arms (was it administered by someone who knew the allocation?), the instrument's minimal important difference, and whether a change of the size claimed is above the noise floor. Lesson 73's point applies unchanged: a statistically significant mean change is not automatically a change anyone would notice.

Four, comparison and delivery. What is 'usual care'? If it meant a waiting list or minimal contact, the estimated benefit includes the non-specific components of the programme — attention, structure, a weekly contact — which a comparison against an active psychological control would remove. And who delivered the programme in the trial: specially trained staff, supervised by the developers, with what caseload? The therapist-effects literature puts about 8.6% of outcome variance with the individual clinician, which is a reason to ask directly whether a real service could staff the same way.

Five, the literature context. One trial, no meta-analysis, so no small-study assessment; a certainty rating for the primary outcome might start at moderate and be rated down for risk of bias (no assessor blinding, developer analysis), imprecision (a single site and modest sample), and indirectness (trial delivery conditions versus routine service), each by a level or more against the explicit criteria, with the final call resting on judgement rather than arithmetic [2]. Note the words used: rated down for stated reasons, not shown to be false.

Six, the system frame. Even if the effect were real and transferable, a commissioning decision depends on reach and displacement: how many of the service's patients could be treated given current clinician hours, what provision would be reduced to fund it, and what happens to those who are not selected. The population figures make the stakes plain — most need is unmet and budgets for mental health are small — which means a new programme usually competes with existing provision rather than adding to it [3].

Conclusion, written with its uncertainty. The programme has one promising trial with a developer interest and an unclear comparator; the direction of benefit is plausible and the size is unestablished; effectiveness against an active comparison is unknown; delivery conditions in routine services would differ from the trial; and commissioning would displace something, which the trial does not measure. What would change this: a second adequately powered trial with pre-registered outcomes, an active comparator matched for attention and contact, independent outcome assessment, and reported fidelity and staffing data. What does not change it: a further satisfaction report or a further single-site replication by the same team. Note that the appraisal has not resolved anything; it has laid out what is load-bearing and what would move it, which is what a reader needs to act or to wait.
lessons.question: A fictional trainee is asked to appraise a claim and produces six headings with a sentence under each, concluding: 'Overall the evidence is mixed, further research is needed.' What is the main defect, in this lesson's terms?
lessons.answer: The appraisal has been performed as ritual: it names no provenance for the load-bearing claims, states no specific unknowns that could be supplied, and offers no revision conditions, so the conclusion is not narrower or more specific than the claim and cannot be acted on or moved by later evidence.
lessons.distractor: The defect is that the trainee reached a conclusion at all; a proper appraisal should report the evidence without evaluating it, so that the reader forms their own judgement.
lessons.correction: Declining to evaluate is not neutrality; it delegates the appraisal to a reader who may be less equipped to do it, and the sources used in this level make judgements explicitly rather than avoiding them — a certainty rating is itself a judgement made against stated criteria, and the handbook's own position is that these are continua requiring judgement rather than a formula [2]. 'Mixed' and 'further research is needed' are true of most bodies of evidence and therefore discriminate nothing. A better conclusion in the same six headings would say which claim the evidence supports, which it does not, which quantities are missing (the comparator-matched effect, the outcome base rate in a comparable population), and what would change the judgement. The trainee's error is not having an opinion; it is having one that cannot be checked, which is the failure this capstone exists to prevent.

depth.definitions:
Claim decomposition: restating an assertion as population, comparator, outcome and time frame, so that evidence can be matched to it. Provenance: the origin and independence of each load-bearing claim, including who funded, conducted and analysed it. Certainty rating: a per-outcome judgement of confidence in an estimate, graded high to very low against explicit named criteria, made by judgement rather than formula [2]. Uncertainty register: the written record of what is unknown, phrased so that it could be supplied, distinguished from what is merely unsatisfying. Revision condition: a statement, made in advance, of the observation that would change the conclusion. Ritual appraisal: a procedure completed in form whose conclusion is unchanged by its own findings. Aleatoric versus epistemic uncertainty: variability inherent in the phenomenon versus uncertainty arising from missing knowledge; the practical difference is that the second shrinks with evidence and the first does not. Competence boundary: the line between understanding an appraisal method and being qualified to make clinical decisions about a person.

Prerequisite: lessons 71-79 in this pack, and the earlier levels' material on formulation, capacity, risk and levels of care. Nothing here replaces clinical training or supervision.
depth.mechanism:
Why this order, and why does each step exist? Each question in the procedure is a check aimed at a documented failure mode, and the order matters because a later question cannot repair an earlier one.

Claim decomposition comes first because unspecified claims cannot be evaluated and because several bundled claims are usually being advanced at once; separating them prevents a strong element from carrying a weak one.

Provenance comes second because the completeness of a record is a property of the record, not of the argument. The regulator-anchored comparison is the model: pooled efficacy was 0.29 in journals against 0.24 in the complete record, with transparency near complete for positive trials and about half for negative ones, improving over cohorts but not to symmetry [1]. A reader who begins with provenance avoids the more laborious error of appraising a biased sample in detail.

Measurement comes third because a change that cannot be detected or does not matter is not evidence of anything, however statistically clean. Invariance, minimal important difference and noise floor are prerequisites for interpreting any comparison (lesson 73).

Comparator and delivery come fourth because an effect is a difference and because staff are part of the intervention; the estimates differ substantively by control condition, and about 8.6% of outcome variance across 27 treatment groups sits with the individual clinician (lesson 78).

Literature context comes fifth because certainty is a property of a body of evidence rather than of one study, and because rating down for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias is how that judgement is made explicit rather than impressionistic [2].

System framing comes sixth because the decision a claim is meant to support usually happens at that level: reach, denominators and displacement determine whether a real effect ever benefits anyone (lesson 79). The population figures — about one in eight people living with a mental disorder, and most people with psychosis outside services — are the scale against which a within-service effect is small [3].

The register of uncertainty is the output. Its discipline is that every unknown must be phrased so that evidence could fill it; 'we cannot know' fails this test, while 'the outcome base rate in this population is unknown, and without it the absolute benefit cannot be estimated' passes it, because someone can go and measure it.
depth.secondExample:
A contrasting pair of write-ups of the same evidence, chosen to show that the difference is not thoroughness but usefulness.

The evidence, in this fictional comparison: a systematic review of fourteen trials of a psychological intervention for a specific anxiety presentation, pooled effect modest, high heterogeneity, seven trials at high risk of bias, no prospectively registered protocol for two-thirds of them, no certainty rating, and a subgroup claim of larger benefit in people with a longer illness duration.

Write-up A concludes: 'The evidence supports the intervention, though further high-quality trials are needed. The subgroup suggests people with longer illness duration benefit more.' It is accurate about the pooled estimate and it contains no false statement. What it does not do is tell the next reader which of its sentences to rely on, and its subgroup sentence has been promoted from exploratory finding to recommendation by the word 'suggests' standing alone.

Write-up B concludes: 'Across fourteen trials the intervention produces a modest average benefit. Because seven trials were at high risk of bias and two-thirds lacked a registered protocol, the pooled estimate should be treated as an upper bound, and no formal assessment of small-study effects was possible with this number of trials, or at best marginal. The subgroup finding was not pre-specified and requires a prior reason to be credible; it is a hypothesis for a prospectively registered trial. What would change this: a pre-registered meta-analysis restricted to low-risk-of-bias trials with a pre-stated primary outcome. What would not: a further high-risk single-site trial.'

Compare what the two write-ups enable. A supports a decision to do nothing further or to act on the pooled number; either is possible and the reader must supply the appraisal themselves. B supports a specific decision and names the evidence that would move it, which means that if someone runs the pre-registered low-risk-of-bias meta-analysis next year, both write-ups' authors can say whether their position changed and on what basis. That audit trail — conclusion, unknown, revision condition — is the practical product of this level. It also has the property of honesty under revision: a writer who has committed to revision conditions cannot quietly reinterpret the new evidence as confirming what they said earlier, because the earlier statement is legible.
depth.mistake:
Misconception one: that a well-conducted appraisal produces a verdict. Its product is a bounded conclusion with a documented uncertainty register; verdicts belong to decision-makers who must also weigh values, resources and consequences, which no evidence base determines.

Misconception two: that documented uncertainty is a failure to decide, so the writer should resolve it for the reader. Write-up A above makes this error in a mild form and is worse for the reader because it invites them to read a subgroup finding as a recommendation. Naming the unknown is the deliverable.

Misconception three: that appraising a body of evidence is the same as evaluating a person's care. It is not, and this is where the education boundary sits. Judgements about an individual — what is happening, whether criteria fit, what would help — depend on information about that person, on clinical training, on supervision and, at times, on legal frameworks, none of which an appraisal method supplies. A learner who becomes fluent in this level can read a paper well and cannot thereby assess or advise a person, and any quiz item in this pack tests the former and never the latter.

Misconception four, at the level of the whole level: that the scepticism taught here is a stance rather than a method. The corrections run in both directions, and the sources do too — reporting transparency improved across cohorts [1], certainty grading separates the strength of a recommendation from the quality of the evidence on which it rests [2], and the appraisal of a service reform has to count substitution rather than assume it. Scepticism that cannot change its mind in the light of better evidence is not method, and the revision condition is what distinguishes the two.

Diagnostic correction: read your own last appraisal and ask whether its conclusion is narrower than the claim that prompted it. If not, either the claim was exceptionally well supported or the procedure was completed without being used.
depth.application:
Capstone task, nonblocking. Assemble an appraisal of the following fictional composite claim in the six-question form, and finish with a three-part uncertainty register (provenance, unknowns, revision conditions), in no more than 400 words. Claim: 'A peer-support programme for people discharged from hospital after a first episode of psychosis reduces readmission by a third and should be adopted across the region.' Available materials, as described: one quasi-experimental before-and-after evaluation at a single site (n = 96) reporting a 33% reduction in readmissions over eighteen months compared with the site's previous two years; a survey in which 88% of participants reported that the programme was 'very helpful'; a regional plan noting that psychiatric bed numbers have fallen by 15% over the same period.

Model response, abbreviated. Claim restated: for people discharged after a first psychotic episode in this region, peer support reduces readmission over eighteen months compared with usual aftercare, by enough to justify regional adoption. Evidence and provenance: a single-site before-and-after comparison and a satisfaction survey. A before-and-after design cannot separate the programme from anything else that changed, and a satisfaction survey cannot estimate an effect; both were produced by the programme's own service, which does not invalidate them but means independence is absent. Measurement: readmission is a routinely recorded administrative outcome, which has the advantage of being complete and the disadvantages that its definition depends on admission criteria and that it responds to bed availability — a 15% fall in regional bed numbers is not a nuisance variable but a competing explanation, since fewer beds produce fewer admissions. Comparison and delivery: the comparison is the same site's previous two years, so any secular change in the service or the population is attributed to the programme; nothing is reported about who delivered the peer support, their training, or the caseload, so fidelity is unknown. Literature context: no synthesis, no registration, no certainty rating; a single-site uncontrolled evaluation with a large reported effect is exactly the pattern that shrinks on better evidence. System: adoption across a region raises denominator and displacement questions — who would be reached, what would fund it, and whether readmission falls because care improved or because admissions were harder to obtain. Uncertainty register. Provenance: site-generated evaluation, no independent analysis, outcome at high risk of detection bias. Unknowns: readmission rate in comparable patients without the programme during the same period; the proportion of eligible people who participated; whether the peer workers were trained and supervised comparably elsewhere. Revision conditions: if a contemporaneous control group with similar bed availability showed no difference, the readmission claim would fall; if a prospectively registered multi-site evaluation replicated a reduction with fidelity data, adoption would become defensible; if bed numbers alone explained the change, the claim would need an outcome other than readmission.

Rubric, five criteria, one point each: (1) the claim is decomposed into population, comparator, outcome and time frame; (2) the design is identified and its specific limitation named rather than dismissed generically; (3) at least one competing explanation is drawn from the supplied materials rather than invented (bed numbers, admission criteria); (4) the uncertainty register contains at least one unknown stated in measurable terms and one revision condition that could actually occur; (5) the conclusion is narrower than the claim. Four or five indicates the level's method is being used; two or fewer usually means the appraisal has produced a verdict instead of a bounded judgement. No score on this task certifies clinical competence, and no answer key in this pack should be read as one.
depth.summary:
The level's method, in one sentence: state the claim, check the provenance of the evidence, examine how it was measured, identify the comparator and the delivery, place it in the literature with its certainty, locate it in a system with its denominators and displacements, and write down what remains unknown and what would change your mind. Its inputs are the description-first method of lessons 71 and 72, the measurement discipline of 73 and 74, the literature appraisal of 75 to 77, the comparator and delivery reasoning of 78, and the system frame of 79.

Three standing limits. First, this method produces bounded judgements, not verdicts, and decisions require values and resources that evidence does not supply. Second, the field's own sources are contested, and the corrections run in both directions: transparency improved over cohorts [1], certainty grading is a judgement against explicit criteria rather than a measurement [2], and the population figures mean that most need never reaches the services where the evidence was gathered [3]. Third, and decisively: nothing in this pack qualifies anyone to diagnose or treat a person. The appraisal skills taught here make a better reader of psychiatric evidence; clinical judgement about an individual requires training, supervision and knowledge of that individual, and a quiz result is not a substitute for any of them.

readings.title: Turner, E. H. et al. (2022), 'Selective publication of antidepressant trials and its influence on apparent efficacy: Updated comparison of 30 trials with FDA drug approval packages', PLoS Medicine 19(1):e1003886
readings.note: Read for the capstone's provenance check: transparent reporting in 15 of 15 positive trials versus 7 of 15 negative trials, FDA-based effect size 0.24 against journal-based 0.29, inflation of 0.05 in the newer cohort against 0.10 in the older, and transparent reporting rising from 11% to 47%. Use it as the demonstration that completeness of the record is measurable — and read the limitations section, which states the paper's own weaknesses.

readings.title: GRADE handbook — sections on rating the certainty of evidence, factors that rate it down, and going from evidence to recommendations
readings.note: Read for the capstone's fifth question: the four certainty categories with their definitions, the named downgrading factors (risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias), and the handbook's statements that the system is not quantitative and that the factors are continua requiring judgement. Also read the section that separates the strength of a recommendation from the quality of the evidence, which is the distinction the capstone's first chapter uses to explain why a trial result does not decide a commissioning question.

readings.title: World Health Organization (2022), 'World mental health report: transforming mental health for all'

readings.title: 'Disturbance of Minimal Self (Ipseity) in Schizophrenia: Clarification and Current Status' — PMC3984529

The capstone uses it to illustrate the general point that every claim has a critical literature, and that an appraisal which has not looked for it has not checked provenance in the full sense.

visual.title: Six labelled appraisal questions and the unknown they leave behind
visual.description: A sequence diagram for the level's capstone method, with each question, the failure it detects, and the specific entry it contributes to the uncertainty register.
steps: Question 1 — What is claimed? Decompose into population, comparator, outcome, time frame. Failure detected: bundled claims in which a strong element carries a weak one. Register entry: which part of the claim is not addressed by the available evidence.

Question 2 — Where did the evidence come from? Provenance: who collected it, on whom, funded and analysed by whom, and is the record complete. Failure detected: appraising in detail a sample that was selected on its results. Register entry: known incompleteness of the source.

Question 3 — How was it measured? Instrument content, invariance across compared groups, noise floor, and the change that would matter to the people involved. Failure detected: treating a statistically significant change as a meaningful one. Register entry: the instrument-specific change threshold that is missing.

Question 4 — Compared with what, delivered by whom? Comparator type and delivery conditions: staffing, supervision, caseload, fidelity. Failure detected: reading an effect against an unstable baseline, or attributing to a technique what the clinician contributed. Register entry: the comparator-matched effect that has not been estimated.

Question 5 — What does the wider literature say? Registration completeness, evidence of selective reporting, whether small-study effects could be assessed at all, and a certainty rating with its named reasons. Failure detected: treating one study as a body of evidence. Register entry: the synthesis or replication that does not yet exist.

Question 6 — In what system must this be true? Denominators, referral and acceptance thresholds, alternate destinations for displaced activity, and who is excluded from the evidence. Failure detected: a real effect that never reaches anyone. Register entry: reach and displacement estimates, plus the population not represented in the evidence. Output: a conclusion narrower than the claim, with revision conditions stated in advance.

questions.prompt: A fictional service wants to use a trial's finding that an intervention reduced relapse by 25% to justify targeting it at 'those most likely to benefit'. The trial's only heterogeneity analysis was an exploratory interaction with symptom duration. What should the service do instead, on this level's evidence?
questions.answer: Use the trial's risk model, if it has one validated for a comparable population, to disaggregate by predicted baseline risk and compute the absolute benefit at each level; if it has none, treat differential benefit as unestablished and base targeting on baseline risk from local data while stating the assumption.
questions.distractor: Re-run the interaction analysis with a more lenient threshold for significance, because the exploratory analysis likely missed a real effect through lack of power and a lower threshold will recover it.
questions.correction: Lowering a threshold increases false positives rather than recovering power, and the underlying problem is not the threshold: interaction tests have much less power than main effects, which is why conventional subgroup analyses are usually unable to detect even large variations in treatment effect, and why the credibility of a subgroup claim depends on a prior probability — even at 80% power, reaching an 80% true positive rate requires a prior of about 20%. Baseline risk is the more productive route because absolute benefit varies with it even when the relative effect is stable, which is what the framework recommends disaggregating on. With a 25% relative reduction, a 40% baseline risk falls to 30% (an absolute reduction of 10 points, NNT about 10) while an 8% risk falls to 6% (2 points, NNT about 50) — the same trial, a fivefold difference in effort per event prevented.

questions.prompt: A fictional journal club discusses a new meta-analysis of nine trials of a treatment for a specific presentation, pooled effect 0.45, and the presenter says the review 'rules out publication bias'. On this level's evidence, what is wrong with that statement, and what would you look for instead?
questions.answer: A nine-study meta-analysis cannot support that conclusion: tests for funnel plot asymmetry should not be used with fewer than about ten studies because power is too low, and asymmetry has causes other than publication bias; look instead for whether unpublished or registered trials were sought, whether the estimate is inflated relative to a complete record, and whether a certainty rating accounts for reporting bias.
questions.distractor: Nothing is wrong, provided the funnel plot was inspected visually, since visual inspection of a funnel plot remains valid at any number of studies even when the formal tests are underpowered.
questions.correction: Visual inspection is not a substitute: the guidance's floor of about ten studies exists because the test's power is insufficient to distinguish chance from real asymmetry, and a visual impression of symmetry in a small set carries no more information than the test does — it can look symmetric while a third of the trials are simply absent. The published-record comparisons give the size of what can be missing: pooled efficacy was 0.29 in journals against 0.24 on the regulator's complete record for newer antidepressants, and adding six unpublished comparisons to twenty published ones reduced a psychological treatment estimate from 0.52 to 0.39, about a quarter. So the answer to 'is there publication bias here' is usually 'plausible and unquantified', and the response is to check the search for registered and unpublished trials and to expect a certainty rating that names reporting bias as a downgrading factor.

questions.prompt: Two fictional trials of the same psychological treatment are reported. Trial P compares it with a waiting list and reports an effect size of 0.8; trial Q compares it with an active control matched for appointment frequency and clinician contact and reports 0.2. A guideline author asks which estimate applies to a service that already offers regular supportive appointments. What is the best answer?
questions.answer: Trial Q's estimate, because the service's realistic alternative already contains the non-specific components — attention, structure and contact — so the relevant question is what the specific package adds to those, and the two trials estimate different quantities rather than the same quantity twice.
questions.distractor: An average of the two estimates, since both are randomised comparisons of the same treatment and averaging them produces a single best estimate of its effect.
questions.correction: Averaging them is the error this lesson exists to catch. The network meta-analysis found effect estimates differ substantively by control condition, and that no-treatment exceeded waiting list with an odds ratio of 2.9 for response — meaning the comparator is not an inert baseline but part of what the difference measures. Trial P's estimate therefore includes the non-specific contribution as well as the specific one, and it is not an independent measurement of the same thing as trial Q's. Two further points belong with the answer: therapist effects contribute about 8.6% of outcome variance across treatment groups, so part of either estimate describes the trial's staff rather than the technique, and researcher allegiance shows a moderate mean association with reported effects of r = .262, so the strength of advocacy around a treatment is a further thing to weigh.

questions.prompt: A fictional commissioning group is told that a new specialist team will treat 500 patients a year in a catchment of 250,000 adults, where the expected prevalence of the target condition is about 4%. The group also hears that the team's evaluation showed a 30% reduction in admissions to the local ward. Which two questions does this level's systems reasoning require before the claim can be accepted?
questions.answer: What proportion of the 10,000 expected cases 500 treated patients represents, and where displaced activity would appear — including beds used out of area, emergency department attendances and readmissions to other providers — since a fall in one setting's admissions may be redistribution rather than reduction.
questions.distractor: Whether the 30% figure was statistically significant in the evaluation and whether the team's clinicians were trained by the model's developers, since these determine whether the effect is real and transferable.
questions.correction: Those two questions are legitimate but they are not the two the systems frame requires. The arithmetic of reach: 4% of 250,000 is 10,000 expected cases, and 500 treated patients is 5% of them — so the team addresses one in twenty of the people the condition affects, which is worth knowing before a 30% effect on admissions is described as a population-level improvement. On displacement: an admission avoided in one ward may be a presentation elsewhere, which is why metrics such as placements outside a provider's own area exist as national statistics; without counting substitute settings, a reduction in one place cannot be distinguished from a shift of activity. The denominator and the displacement map are the two questions the correction names, and the statistical and training questions can be asked afterwards.

questions.prompt: A fictional appraisal of a treatment claim ends: 'The evidence base is heterogeneous and limited; on balance the intervention is probably effective and further research would be welcome.' Which single addition would most improve it, in this level's terms?
questions.answer: A named unknown phrased so it could be measured, together with a revision condition — for example, the comparator-matched effect in a population like this service's, and the finding that would falsify the conclusion — so that later evidence can move the judgement rather than be absorbed as confirmation.
questions.distractor: A certainty rating using all four GRADE categories, because a formal grade would supply the precision that the sentence lacks and make the appraisal complete.
questions.correction: A grade is useful and it is not the missing element: certainty grading is a judgement made against explicit criteria, expressed in four levels with named reasons for rating down, and the handbook is explicit that these are continua decided by judgement rather than a formula — so a grade would document the appraisal rather than sharpen it beyond what it already says. What the sentence lacks is anything that could be supplied or contradicted: 'heterogeneous and limited' and 'probably effective' cannot be checked, and 'further research would be welcome' names no study. Adding the specific unknown (the comparator-matched effect, the outcome base rate in a comparable population) and the revision condition turns the paragraph into something a later reader can use and audit — which is the test of an appraisal given in the capstone, namely whether the conclusion is narrower than the claim and able to change.

questions.prompt: A fictional research team reports that a five-item experience scale has internal consistency of 0.91, test-retest reliability of 0.85, and a factor structure matching its published form. Their paper proposes the scale as a clinical screening tool for a specific perceptual anomaly. Using this level's treatment of description, instruments and measurement, what has the team established and what has it not?
questions.answer: It has established consistency and structure — the items hang together, the scores repeat when nothing has changed, and the scale behaves like a one-dimensional measure — but not that the scale codes the anomaly as described, not that its scores behave equivalently across the groups it would be used with, and not what a score or a change in it means.
questions.distractor: It has established that the scale measures the anomaly, since a high internal consistency combined with a stable factor structure and reliable retest scores is the standard evidence that a scale is unidimensional and therefore specific to the construct it was designed for.
questions.correction: Work through what each statistic can and cannot do. Internal consistency shows items covary, which is satisfied by near-duplicate items as easily as by a well-specified construct. Test-retest reliability shows stability, and a scale can be stably measuring the wrong thing. A factor structure shows the items form a coherent dimension in that sample, which is a claim about dimensionality and not about content: the observationally critical question has not been asked, which is what the items code — the person's own description of the mode of the experience, or their willingness to endorse a phrase. Beyond those, two omissions matter for a screening claim: invariance (does the item behave the same at equal underlying severity across languages and clinical groups, a check the four-country PHQ-9 study demonstrates and which is what permits a mean difference to be read as a difference in the construct) and interpretability (what score or change matters, which requires an anchor from outside the scale). Finally, description-first method is not decoration here: if the scale codes themes rather than modes, it cannot distinguish experiences that differ in form, which is where much of the classificatory weight sits.

questions.prompt: A fictional early-intervention service proposes to use a phenomenological instrument to decide who receives a preventive intervention, citing a follow-up study in a high-risk sample in which the instrument's total score predicted shorter time to onset in a Cox model controlling for other predictors, and a diagnostic study in which scores aggregated in one spectrum. Write the reasoning that should decide whether the service can do this.
questions.answer: Neither study supplies what a selection rule needs: a threshold with measured sensitivity and specificity, the outcome base rate in a population like the service's, and the proportions above and below the cut-off who go on to develop the outcome, plus evidence that the instrument adds information beyond standard assessment. The prediction model was estimated in a small single cohort, and aggregation by group is not specificity for an individual.
questions.distractor: Neither study design can be used because a Cox model estimated in a high-risk sample and a cross-sectional comparison of diagnostic groups are observational rather than experimental, and only randomised evidence can support a decision about who should receive an intervention.
questions.correction: The distractor applies a rule that does not exist and would rule out most of clinical reasoning: risk prediction legitimately comes from prospective cohort data, and the issue with these studies is not that they lack randomisation but what quantities they report. The first answer names the actual gap. A prediction coefficient, even a significant one, does not identify the individual: converting a model to a decision requires a threshold, the distribution of scores and outcomes around it, and the positive and negative predictive values that follow from the outcome's base rate in the target population — arithmetic that lesson 65 set out. Sample size and design matter too: a follow-up of a few dozen high-risk participants with a mean of about eighteen months cannot support calibration for a service. And the specificity question is unresolved in the field's own literature, which notes that closely related disturbances occur in other conditions and that the relevant comparisons had not been made. The defensible decision: use the instrument in research or to structure a conversation, and do not let a score allocate a preventive intervention.

questions.prompt: A fictional guidelines committee is choosing between a long-established diagnostic category and a proposed replacement. Evidence presented for the replacement: better agreement between raters (kappa 0.62 versus 0.45 under the study's own design), narrower criteria, and a supporting narrative from clinical experts. Evidence against: no follow-up or family study has compared the two. What should the committee's reasoning be?
questions.answer: Agreement is a reliability result and does not adjudicate between the two categories on validity; the missing element is a head-to-head comparison under validators agreed in advance — course, family aggregation, treatment response — showing that the replacement performs better, and reliance on expert narrative reintroduces exactly the top-down expert classification that the validation programme was designed to replace.
questions.distractor: The replacement should be adopted because a kappa of 0.62 crosses the conventional threshold for substantial agreement while 0.45 sits only in the moderate range, and reliability is the primary evidence for a psychiatric diagnosis.
questions.correction: The threshold claim is fragile in this field for a documented reason: reliability estimates for the same manual can differ substantially by the method used, with mean kappa 0.80 under audio-recorded review against 0.47 under test-retest in one programme and about a quarter of test-retest estimates classed as poor. If the same categories can score 0.45 or 0.62 depending on whether the second assessment is a recording review or a fresh interview, a comparison across two categories using one method is not decisive — and the committee should ask what method was used in each arm. The deeper point is the axis mismatch: reliability is agreement between clinicians, validity is whether the category picks out a coherent group, and the field's own standard for revision is evidence that the new criteria improve on the predecessor under an agreed set of validators. Expert narrative, meanwhile, is precisely the input whose unreliability motivated operational criteria, as the historical account of nineteenth-century nosology shows.

questions.prompt: A fictional trainee drafts a paragraph: 'Three meta-analyses report that this intervention works, with pooled effects of 0.4 to 0.6. Because synthesis is at the top of the evidence hierarchy, the intervention is established.' Rewrite the appraisal in this level's terms, naming the checks that determine how much the pooled figure can bear.
questions.answer: Pooled effects of 0.4 to 0.6 across three syntheses can be an arithmetic summary of a selected sample: the checks are whether unpublished and registered trials were sought, whether the trials were prospectively registered and their outcomes pre-specified, whether the number of studies permitted any assessment of small-study effects, whether the certainty of the estimate was rated with named reasons for rating down, and whether the three syntheses draw on overlapping studies so that 'three' may describe one literature rather than three independent bodies of evidence.
questions.distractor: The paragraph is sound in its structure; the remaining checks concern only the internal quality of the individual trials, such as blinding and allocation concealment, because synthesis removes the problem of how the included studies were selected.
questions.correction: The distractor inverts the actual difficulty: synthesis is arithmetic over the studies that exist, so selection is the problem synthesis cannot solve — it can only fail to detect it. The measured size of the effect of selection is available: pooled efficacy for newer antidepressants was 0.29 based on journals against 0.24 based on the regulator's complete record, and adding six unpublished comparisons to twenty published ones moved a psychological-treatment estimate from 0.52 to 0.39, a reduction of about a quarter. Detection is also limited by arithmetic: tests for funnel-plot asymmetry should not be used below about ten studies, and the minimum rises when heterogeneity is substantial, so many psychiatric syntheses cannot support a claim either way. Overlap is the third check: three meta-analyses of one literature are one body of evidence counted three times, and overlap needs to be controlled or reported. Certainty grading then records the judgement about the estimate, per outcome, with named reasons for rating down — which is a judgement against explicit criteria, not a measurement.

questions.prompt: A fictional guideline recommends an intervention on the basis of a 20% relative reduction in a serious event, and a service with a caseload spanning a wide range of baseline risks asks how to describe the benefit to two different people: one with an estimated two-year event risk of 50%, the other 5%. Compute the absolute effects and state what follows for how the recommendation should be presented.
questions.answer: At a 50% baseline risk the absolute reduction is 10 percentage points, an NNT of about 10; at 5% it is 1 percentage point, an NNT of about 100. The same trial supports a materially different statement for each person, so the recommendation should be presented with absolute benefits at the relevant baseline risk rather than as a single relative reduction.
questions.distractor: At both risk levels the reduction is 20%, so the honest presentation is the relative figure, which is the trial's actual finding and therefore the most faithful thing to communicate to either person.
questions.correction: The relative figure is faithful to the trial and incomplete for the decision — which is the distinction the whole of this level's treatment half rests on. The arithmetic, shown so it can be checked: a 20% relative reduction applied to 50% gives 40% (absolute reduction 10 points; NNT = 1/0.10 = 10), and applied to 5% gives 4% (absolute reduction 1 point; NNT = 1/0.01 = 100). That tenfold difference in effort per event prevented comes from baseline risk alone, with no interaction and no subgroup hunting — which is why disaggregation by predicted risk is recommended over effect-modification claims, and why the credibility of subgroup claims depends on a prior probability that sparse psychiatric literatures rarely supply. Two qualifications belong in the same breath: the baseline risk estimates require a validated model for a comparable population, and a decision also needs the harms and burdens at each risk level, since an NNT describes benefit only.

questions.prompt: A fictional formulary paper concludes: 'Certainty of evidence is low for this outcome, so the intervention does not work for it.' Which reformulation is correct, and what should the certainty rating have been doing?
questions.answer: Low certainty means the estimate could easily be different — it may be compatible with a worthwhile benefit, with no effect, or with harm — and the rating should record which named factors were rated down (risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias) so that a decision can weigh the plausible range rather than a verdict.
questions.distractor: Low certainty is equivalent to no recommendation at all, so a formulary committee should defer the decision until certainty rises to moderate or high rather than reasoning about a low-certainty estimate.
questions.correction: Deferral sounds cautious and is itself a decision, made on the basis of an estimate that has been rated and can be read: an imprecise estimate whose confidence interval spans a clinically worthwhile benefit and no effect is exactly the information a committee needs for a judgement about cost, burden and alternatives — which is why the system separates the strength of a recommendation from the certainty of the evidence. The reformulation also matters with respect to the words used: 'rated down for imprecision' is a statement about the interval, not about the treatment, and 'rated down for publication bias' is a statement about the literature's completeness. Note the plausible-range point by contrast with the arithmetic question before this one: at a plausible 20% relative reduction, an estimate compatible with anywhere between a 5% and a 33% reduction still includes a material absolute benefit for high-risk patients, so reading it as nothing removes the very information that would justify a conditional recommendation.

questions.prompt: A fictional service decides to adopt a therapy whose trials reported an effect size of 0.7 against waiting list. Six months after adoption, routine outcomes show no improvement relative to the service's previous year. List the explanations this level's evidence would put in order, and say what each implies for what to measure next.
questions.answer: Start with the trial's comparator and delivery: the 0.7 estimate was against a waiting list, so part of it was non-specific improvement that routine care may already provide; then fidelity and staffing, since about 8.6% of outcome variance sits with the individual clinician and the trial's therapists were likely trained and supervised differently; then measurement, since routine outcomes may use a different instrument or a change threshold below the noise floor; and only then entertain that the treatment effect is absent.
questions.distractor: Conclude that the trial result was fraudulent or that the therapy does not work, since routine service data are the strongest available test of an intervention once it is in use.
questions.correction: Routine service data cannot test an intervention: without a comparison group and a denominator they cannot separate treatment effect from regression to the mean, spontaneous fluctuation, case-mix change and expectancy, and a fall in admissions or a flat symptom score in a service is compatible with several of those at once. The ordered explanations follow from the evidence in this level. Comparator first: the network meta-analysis found estimates differ substantively by control condition, and that no treatment exceeded waiting list for response with an odds ratio of 2.9, so a waiting-list comparison builds in the non-specific elements that ordinary care supplies. Delivery second: therapist variance of about 8.6% across treatment groups is larger than many treatment contrasts, so fidelity, supervision and caseload need measuring, not assuming. Measurement third: a service using a different scale than the trial, without invariance or interpretability evidence, is not measuring the same thing. What to measure next, in that order: comparator-matched outcomes with a contemporaneous comparison, fidelity and therapist-level variance, and the instrument's change threshold — with researcher allegiance borne in mind as a reason the original estimate may have been optimistic.

questions.prompt: A fictional region has reduced inpatient beds by 15% and increased community team capacity. Two years later, admissions are down 18%, out-of-area placements are up 40%, and the number of people in contact with services is unchanged. Write the systems reading of those three numbers and the one measurement that would most clarify them.
questions.answer: The pattern is consistent with redistribution and threshold shifting rather than reduced need: fewer local admissions and more placements outside the area suggests activity moved rather than disappeared, while unchanged contact numbers suggests the community capacity has not increased overall reach; the most clarifying measurement is the total number of bed-days used across all providers including out-of-area, plus the local admission criteria in each period.
questions.distractor: The pattern shows the community reform succeeded, since admissions are the outcome the reform targeted and they fell by more than the beds removed, while out-of-area placements are an administrative matter relating to bed availability elsewhere in the region.
questions.correction: Admissions falling further than beds were removed is exactly what redistribution looks like: with local beds scarcer, admission becomes harder (a threshold shift) and those still admitted are a more selected group, while patients who cannot be placed locally go outside the area, which is why such placements are collected as a national statistic. Treating them as administrative is the error the systems material warns against, because they are where displaced need becomes visible. The unchanged contact numbers are the most informative of the three: if community capacity had increased reach, contact should rise against a stable or rising population, so the reform appears to have changed how the same people are served rather than how many are served — a legitimate aim, but a different claim from reducing need. The clarifying measurement: total bed-days across all providers, including out-of-area, compared with the baseline, together with the local admission criteria in each period and the referral and acceptance rates that determine the denominator.

questions.prompt: You are asked to appraise: 'A randomised trial of 300 patients found that a structured intervention reduced symptom scores by 4 points more than treatment as usual; the developers, who ran the trial, report that the difference exceeded the scale's minimal important difference; the intervention is recommended for routine use.' Identify the four decisive checks and the one that most changes the conclusion.
questions.answer: Whether the minimal important difference estimate belongs to this instrument administered in this way at the relevant baseline severity; whether the trial was prospectively registered with the reported outcome pre-specified, given the developer's interest; whether treatment as usual contained the non-specific elements the intervention also supplies; and whether the delivery conditions — staff training, supervision, caseload — could be reproduced in routine services. The check that most changes the conclusion is the minimal important difference, because the entire claimed benefit rests on that threshold.
questions.distractor: Whether the trial's sample of 300 was large enough to detect a 4-point difference, since a p value below 0.05 demonstrates that the difference is real and the remaining questions are questions of interpretation rather than of whether the effect exists.
questions.correction: Statistical significance is the least informative of the available checks here: with 300 participants a 4-point difference can be precisely estimated and yet not matter, and precision says nothing about whether the right quantity was measured. The four checks follow the capstone's order. Measurement first: minimal important differences are instrument-, anchor-, population- and severity-specific — one primary-care study estimated thresholds of about 1.7 points on one questionnaire while a different study of another instrument in different trial populations gave 3 to 4 T-score points — so 'exceeded the minimal important difference' must specify whose estimate and where. Provenance second: a developer-run trial with no mention of registration needs its pre-specification checked, since transparency has been shown to be near complete for positive trials and about half for negative ones in the regulatory comparison. Comparator third: 'treatment as usual' may itself contain attention, structure and expectancy, in which case the difference understates the package and overstates the specific technique. Delivery fourth: about 8.6% of outcome variance across treatment groups sits with the individual clinician, so routine adoption assumes comparable staffing and supervision.

questions.prompt: Two fictional studies of the same diagnostic interview report agreement of 0.78 and 0.34. The second study used the same interview but had the second assessment conducted by a fresh interviewer without access to the first set of notes. A guideline developer asks which figure to use. What reasoning does this level supply, and what else about the interview would you want to know?
questions.answer: Both figures are valid estimates of different things: agreement depends on the method — recorded review versus a fresh independent assessment — and on the heterogeneity of the sample, so the guideline should report both with their methods rather than choosing one; what is still needed is the distribution of the condition in each sample, since agreement is harder to achieve when prevalence is low, and whether the interview's categories were applied by clinicians trained to a common standard.
questions.distractor: The higher figure should be used, because the second study's method was less standard and fresh interviewers without access to previous notes cannot be expected to reach the same diagnosis reliably.
questions.correction: The reverse inference is the interesting one: a fresh independent assessment without access to earlier notes is a more demanding test of the instrument's informational content, and the falling figure is not an artefact of bad procedure but a measurement of how much of the first assessment's conclusion depended on the conversation that produced it. The level's evidence shows how large this dependence can be within one programme — mean kappa 0.80 under audio-recorded review against 0.47 under test-retest, with about a quarter of test-retest estimates classed as poor, and a public dispute over which benchmark to apply that did not dispute the numbers. Two further properties of agreement statistics matter here: kappa is affected by the base rate of the condition, so low-prevalence samples tend to produce lower values without the interview being worse, and choosing between values requires knowing sample composition. This is the same reasoning that applies to a rating scale, where consistency, structure, invariance and interpretability are separate properties rather than one quantity.

questions.prompt: A fictional clinician reads two reports of the same person's experience. The first records: 'Patient reports that thoughts are inserted; no insight.' The second records: 'Says thoughts arrive already spoken, in a voice that is not his, though he says they come from his own head; when asked whether that makes the thoughts his, says he does not know what would make a thought his.' Using this level's material, assess the two records and what each can support.
questions.answer: The second preserves the person's words, separates the description from any judgement, and adds a distinction the first has hidden — the experience is estranged in its mode while its spatial origin remains his own, and his uncertainty concerns ownership rather than the fact of the experience — so it supports clinical reasoning about the form of the experience while the first supports only a conclusion, and neither supports a diagnosis.
questions.distractor: The first is the better clinical record because it is concise and uses standard terminology, which allows another clinician to reproduce the same assessment; the second is idiosyncratic and risks being misinterpreted by a reader who does not know the person.
questions.correction: Standard terminology is what makes the first record easy to reproduce and is exactly why it is uninformative: a checkbox phrased in technical terms cannot be checked by the reader, and it has absorbed two distinct findings — an altered mode of experience and a judgement of doubtful insight — into a single term, in the manner lesson 63 warned about when it distinguished what is reported from what is observed. The second record earns its length by keeping the person's own phrasing and marking the boundary between the description and any inference, and it captures something the first erased: that his own sense of the experience is uncertain in a specific way, which is precisely the kind of form-level detail that carries classificatory weight. What neither supports is a diagnosis, or a claim about the person's future; description informs reasoning rather than settling it, and the same descriptive pattern can occur in more than one clinical context.

questions.prompt: Assemble the reasoning for this decision: a fictional service with 4,000 people on its caseload wants to commission a new intensive intervention based on one positive randomised trial conducted in a different country, and the trial's own service had one trained clinician per 40 patients while this service has one per 120. Write the four-part assessment and the single cheapest measurement that would most reduce the uncertainty.
questions.answer: One: the evidence is a single trial, so provenance and pre-specification should be checked before the effect size is used at all. Two: the comparator and outcome definitions must match the local alternative, or the estimate will not transfer. Three: staffing is part of the intervention — one clinician per 40 versus one per 120 is a different treatment, so fidelity, caseload and supervision will determine whether the effect is even available here. Four: capacity and displacement decide reach: with limited capacity the intervention can serve a fraction of the caseload and will displace whatever currently fills those clinician hours. The cheapest uncertainty-reducing measurement is the service's own current outcome and contact data by clinician, which establishes the local baseline and shows how much clinician-level variance exists, allowing the trial effect to be read against local delivery conditions.
questions.distractor: The cheapest and most decisive step is to survey the caseload about their willingness to try the new intervention, since adoption is only worthwhile if the people concerned are willing to participate and satisfaction is the outcome most relevant to them.
questions.correction: Willingness is worth knowing and it answers none of the four questions: a service can be full of willing patients and still lack the clinician hours to deliver ten sessions each, and satisfaction measures what people think of what they receive rather than what changed. The four-part assessment is the capstone's order applied to a commissioning decision, and each part has a specific failure mode available in the evidence. Provenance: a single positive trial by its own developers is the pattern whose published record was least improved in the regulatory comparison, where 100% of positive trials were transparently reported against 47% of negative ones. Comparator: estimates differ substantively by control condition, so 'the local alternative' has to be named before the effect is quoted. Fidelity: about 8.6% of outcome variance sits with the individual clinician in the review evidence, and caseload is a delivery variable rather than an administrative one, so the 40-versus-120 difference is part of the intervention. Capacity and reach: with 4,000 people on the caseload the arithmetic of clinician hours decides how many can be treated and what stops — the same computation that shows a ten-session intervention delivered by a handful of clinicians reaches a small minority of those the evidence might apply to.
